context: The magma's heat changes the limestone beside it into marble, a stone long used for statues and buildings. Slate and quartzite come from other rocks, and granite is the kind of rock the magma itself can harden into.

question: Slate is a grey rock that splits into thin, flat sheets, so it has long been used for roof tiles and school blackboards. Heat and pressure made it out of an older rock. Which rock was slate before?
answer: Shale
choices: Shale
Limestone
Sandstone
Basalt
context: Slate begins as shale, a rock of hardened mud. Heat and pressure make it harder and denser, and it splits cleanly into smooth sheets, which is why it makes good roof tiles.

question: Deep in the roots of a mountain range lies rock that heat and pressure made out of an older rock long ago. Now it grows hot enough to begin melting, and the melt rises and hardens into granite. Which change of the rock cycle is this last step?
answer: Metamorphic rock becoming igneous rock
choices: Metamorphic rock becoming igneous rock
Metamorphic rock becoming sedimentary rock
Sedimentary rock becoming igneous rock
Sedimentary rock becoming metamorphic rock
context: Rock that heat and pressure have made is metamorphic rock, and once rock melts, the melt that cools and hardens is igneous rock, whatever it was before. So the last step turns metamorphic rock into igneous rock, one of many paths through the rock cycle, which runs in no fixed order.

question: Geologists sort all of Earth's rocks into just three great kinds. What decides which kind a rock belongs to?
answer: How the rock formed
choices: How the rock formed
How hard the rock is
What colour the rock is
How old the rock is
context: Igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rock are each named for the way a rock formed, and colour, hardness and age can only be clues. A dark rock, for instance, can be igneous like basalt, sedimentary like coal, or metamorphic like slate.

question: Far from any coast, the floor of the open ocean lies kilometres down in darkness. Most of the solid rock that forms it is of one kind. Which rock is it?
answer: Basalt
choices: Basalt
Granite
Limestone
Obsidian
context: The crust under the open ocean is made mostly of basalt, from lava that flowed out onto the sea floor and hardened there. Granite is common in the crust of the continents, limestone forms mostly from shells and coral in warm, shallow seas, and obsidian is a glassy rock made from a different kind of lava.

question: Scientists who study the air find harmful gases and tiny specks of pollution over cities and countryside alike. Most of the polluted air that people breathe comes from one kind of activity. What is it?
answer: Burning fuels such as coal, gasoline and wood
choices: Burning fuels such as coal, gasoline and wood
Spraying farm fields with fertiliser and weedkiller
Digging coal and rock out of open mines
Burying rubbish and food scraps in landfills
context: Burning coal, oil, gas and wood in engines, power plants, factories and home stoves gives off soot and gases such as carbon monoxide, nitrogen dioxide and sulfur dioxide. It makes about 85 percent of the polluted air people breathe, so farms, mines, landfills and everything else together add a much smaller share.

question: Smoke from a great forest fire drifts over a town and turns the sky hazy. The smoke is a mixture of gases, among them carbon dioxide and carbon monoxide, and bits of soot and ash of every size. Health agencies warn that one part of it is the biggest threat to health. Which part?
answer: The finest specks of soot and ash
choices: The finest specks of soot and ash
The largest flakes of soot and ash
The carbon monoxide gas
The carbon dioxide gas
context: The finest specks, under 2.5 thousandths of a millimetre across and about 30 times thinner than a hair, slip past the nose and throat deep into the lungs, and some pass into the blood. Larger flakes usually never reach the lungs, though they sting the eyes and throat. Carbon monoxide is a danger close to the flames but is found only in very low amounts a short way from them, and carbon dioxide is not among the pollutants the World Health Organization names as the most worrying.

question: A tanker wreck can spill thousands of tonnes of oil into the sea at once. Yet a 2022 study of the seas around North America found that more oil reaches them in another way, a little at a time. What was the biggest source?
answer: Rain washing oil off roads and parking lots
choices: Rain washing oil off roads and parking lots
Oil seeping up through cracks in the seabed
Ships pumping oily waste water overboard
Small, steady leaks from offshore oil rigs
context: Rain and melting snow wash oil from leaking cars, roads and parking lots into drains and rivers, and the rivers carry it to the sea; a National Academies report in 2022 ranked this runoff from the land first. Natural seeps from the seabed came second and spills third, and the oily discharges of ships are small.

question: At a drinking-water plant, river water is cleaned in several steps on its way to people's taps. Near the end, workers add a small, carefully measured dose of chlorine. What is the chlorine for?
answer: To kill any germs left in the water
choices: To kill any germs left in the water
To make specks of dirt clump and sink
To keep the water pipes from rusting
To remove minerals that make water hard
context: Chlorine kills the germs that the filters did not catch, and a little is left in the water so it keeps killing germs in the pipes on the way to the taps. Water can look perfectly clear and still carry germs too small to see. Alum makes the dirt clump and sink near the start, and softening hard water and protecting pipes are separate treatments.

question: At a sewage treatment plant, dirty water from a town's drains flows into long, deep tanks, and pumps bubble air through it for hours. What is the air for?
answer: It brings oxygen to bacteria that eat the waste
choices: It brings oxygen to bacteria that eat the waste
It kills off the bacteria that live in the waste
It cools the water before it flows to a river
It helps the heavy solid waste sink to the bottom
context: Bacteria in the tanks feed on the waste and break it down, and like people they need oxygen to do it, so the plant keeps them alive and even sends some back into the tanks to keep their numbers up. The heavy solids were already left to sink in tanks of still water. Untreated sewage spreads diseases such as cholera and typhoid, and its rotting uses up the oxygen in rivers.

question: After the harvest, a farmer leaves the dead straw and stalks of her crop lying on the field instead of ploughing the ground bare. In the next heavy storm, her field loses far less soil than the bare field next door. What does the straw do?
answer: It takes the blow of the falling raindrops
choices: It takes the blow of the falling raindrops
It keeps the rain from soaking into the soil
It pins the soil down under its weight
It packs the soil into a hard crust
context: Raindrops hit bare soil hard enough to knock specks loose and splash them away, and the splashed specks clog the surface into a crust, so less rain soaks in and more runs off, carrying soil with it. Straw takes the blow of each drop, so the surface stays open and more rain soaks in, not less. It shields the soil rather than weighing it down.

question: On flat, open farmland, farmers plant long rows of trees along the edges of their fields. In dry years the soil in those fields stays put, while open fields nearby lose much of theirs. What do the rows of trees do that saves the soil?
answer: They slow the wind across the fields
choices: They slow the wind across the fields
Their roots hold the soil across the fields
Their fallen leaves cover the bare soil
They draw more rain to the dry fields
context: A row of trees, called a windbreak, can cut the wind's speed by half or more close behind the row and shelters the soil for 10 to 20 times its own height downwind, and slower wind cannot lift and carry off the dry soil. The trees' roots reach only a narrow strip of the field near the row. After the dust storms of the 1930s, about 220 million trees were planted in such rows across the American plains.

question: An old-style incandescent bulb lights up when electricity flows through a thin wire inside it. Many homes now use light-emitting diode (LED) bulbs instead. What becomes of the electrical energy that the old bulb takes in?
answer: Most becomes heat, and a little becomes light
choices: Most becomes heat, and a little becomes light
Most becomes light, and a little becomes heat
About half becomes light, and half becomes heat
Most becomes light, and the rest is used up
context: More than 90 percent of the energy an old incandescent bulb takes in leaves it as heat, and only about a tenth or less becomes light. An LED turns far less of its energy into heat, so a 9-watt LED gives about the same light as a 60-watt old bulb. Energy is never used up: it only changes from one form to another.

question: A boy wonders whether the length of a paper plane's wings changes how far it glides. Before he folds a single plane, he writes in his notebook: "If a paper plane has longer wings, then it will glide farther." What has he written?
answer: A hypothesis
choices: A hypothesis
A theory
A law
A model
context: A hypothesis is a testable idea about what will happen, often written as "if..., then...", and folding planes with short and long wings and measuring their glides will test it. A law or a theory rests on a great many tests already done, and a model is a copy or picture of something, such as a globe.

question: A man says that a fire-breathing dragon lives in his garage. His friend sees nothing there, but the dragon is invisible, the man explains. Flour on the floor would show no footprints, since the dragon floats, and a heat camera would find nothing, since its fire gives off no heat. Why is his claim not a scientific hypothesis?
answer: No test could ever show it to be wrong
choices: No test could ever show it to be wrong
No scientist has proven it to be true
It is not written as an if-then sentence
It is about a dragon, a creature of old stories
context: A scientific hypothesis must be testable: some observation has to be able to tell whether it is right. Every test the friend can think of meets a new excuse, so no evidence could ever count against the dragon; a dragon that left footprints in the flour would be a claim science could check. The astronomer Carl Sagan told this tale in The Demon-Haunted World and asked how such a dragon differs from no dragon at all.

question: Ravi's hypothesis says that a can of water painted black warms up faster in sunshine than one painted white. He tests ten pairs of cans on five sunny days, and every time the black can warms faster. What can he now say about his hypothesis?
answer: His results support it
choices: His results support it
His results prove it true for good
His results tell nothing about it yet
His results count for nothing until he knows why
context: Results that agree with a hypothesis support it, even before anyone can explain why it holds. Science does not call an idea proven for good, since a later test under other conditions could still find a case where it fails, so scientists keep testing even well-supported ideas.

question: Told to wash his hands before dinner, a boy shrugs. Germ theory, the idea that many illnesses are caused by germs too small to see, is only a theory, he says, and a theory is just a guess. What does "theory" mean to a scientist?
answer: A well-tested explanation of how nature works
choices: A well-tested explanation of how nature works
A guess that is still waiting for its first test
An idea one step short of becoming a law
A rule that has been proven true forever
context: In everyday speech a theory can be a hunch, but to a scientist it is an explanation backed by a large body of evidence from many tests over many years. Germ theory has more than a century of such evidence behind it, from the work of Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch onward. A theory does not turn into a law, and science calls no idea proven forever.

question: Isaac Newton's law of gravity, published in 1687, applies to every pair of masses, from an apple and Earth to the Sun and its planets. Yet in a later edition of his book, Newton wrote that one thing about gravity was still beyond him. What did his law leave unexplained?
answer: What causes the pull of gravity
choices: What causes the pull of gravity
How strongly two masses pull each other
How the pull weakens with distance
Which way the pull of gravity acts
context: A law describes what happens, here how strongly two masses pull on each other and how the pull weakens with distance, without saying why. Newton wrote that he had not been able to discover the cause of gravity's properties, and he refused to make up a guess. More than two centuries later, Albert Einstein's general relativity, a theory, explained gravity as mass bending space and time.

question: When a sealed-in gas is squeezed into half the space at the same temperature, its pressure doubles. Scientists found this pattern in the 1600s and call it a law. The particle theory of gases accounts for it: crowded closer, the gas's moving particles strike the walls more often. Will the theory one day become a law?
answer: No, for the two do different jobs
choices: No, for the two do different jobs
Yes, once it has been tested enough
Yes, once it is written as an equation
No, for only a law can be written as an equation
context: A law describes a pattern and a theory explains why it happens, so neither grows into the other. The gas law, Boyle's law, goes back to Robert Boyle's measurements of 1662, and the particle theory is still a theory after more than 150 years of tests. The theory even has equations of its own.

question: The Mars Climate Orbiter, an American spacecraft, reached Mars in September 1999, flew far too low into the planet's air and was lost. Engineers at the company that built it had sent the mission's navigators figures for every small thruster firing. What did the review board find wrong with those figures?
answer: They were in English units, not metric
choices: They were in English units, not metric
They were rounded off far too roughly
They had two digits swapped by mistake
They came from a faulty thruster sensor
context: The builders' software gave each thruster's push in pound-force seconds, an English unit, while the navigators' software expected newton-seconds, the metric unit, so the craft's path was worked out wrong and it passed only about 57 kilometres above Mars. Mix-ups like this are why scientists everywhere share one system of units, the International System (SI), the modern metric system.

question: A lab worker draws 5 millilitres of blue dye into a syringe, ready to add to a test tube. What part of a litre is one millilitre?
answer: A thousandth of a litre
choices: A thousandth of a litre
A millionth of a litre
A hundredth of a litre
A tenth of a litre
context: The prefix milli- comes from the Latin word mille, a thousand, and means a thousandth: 1,000 millilitres fill a litre, just as 1,000 millimetres make a metre. Milli- sounds like million, but a millionth takes the prefix micro-, and a hundredth takes centi-.

question: A biologist kneels beside a pond and writes in her field notebook that the water is cloudy and green and smells of rotten eggs. What has she recorded?
answer: Qualitative data
choices: Qualitative data
Quantitative data
An inference
A prediction
context: Qualitative data are descriptions in words, such as colour, smell or texture, while quantitative data are measurements in numbers, such as the water's temperature in degrees Celsius; both count as evidence. Her note records what she saw and smelled, not a conclusion drawn from it (an inference) or a guess about what will happen (a prediction).

question: A student rolls a toy car down the same ramp five times and measures how far it travels across the floor. Four runs reach between 118 and 121 centimetres, but one stops at 64 centimetres. What should she do about that short run?
answer: Look for a cause, then run that trial again
choices: Look for a cause, then run that trial again
Erase it from her notes, as it spoils the pattern
Average it in with the other four, just as it is
Run the four long trials again to check them
context: A result far from the rest, called an outlier, may be a fluke or a slip, such as a misread tape measure or a car that clipped a chair leg, so she looks for the cause and repeats that trial. She keeps the odd result in her notes and says what she did with it, because quietly dropping data misleads. Averaged in as it stands, the short run would drag her result far below what the car really does, and the four runs that agree need no rerun.

question: Two groups take turns timing the same pendulum through ten swings, and each group runs five trials. One group's times all lie within a fifth of a second of one another, while the other group's are spread across three seconds. Which group's result can the class trust more?
answer: The group whose times agree closely
choices: The group whose times agree closely
The group whose spread shows how the swings really vary
Either group, as each one ran five trials
Neither group, as both groups' times vary
context: Trials of the same measurement should agree, and when they do, the result can be trusted to come out the same again. A pendulum keeps very nearly the same time swing after swing, so a wide spread comes from the measuring, such as a slip in counting the swings, and that group should find the cause and run more trials. A little spread is normal, and close agreement is still no proof of a right answer, since a faulty tool can be off by the same amount every time.

question: A student times a toy car rolling down a ramp, five runs in all, and her five times differ a little. She takes the average of the five as her result. Why is the average more trustworthy than the time of any one run?
answer: It lets too-long and too-short times partly cancel
choices: It lets too-long and too-short times partly cancel
It picks out the run she timed most carefully
It shows just how far apart her five times are
It gives the car's true time, with no error left at all
context: Chance slips make some times a little too long and others a little too short, so in an average they partly cancel, and no single slip sways the result much. Every run she keeps goes into the average, and the average does not show how far apart the times are: that is the spread. No number of runs takes away every error.

question: A class measures how much water evaporates in a week from four matching dishes set side by side on a sunny windowsill. One dish has a hairline crack, and water slowly seeps out through it. When the class measures the water left in that dish, what will the dish's result seem to show?
answer: More evaporation than really happened
choices: More evaporation than really happened
Less evaporation than really happened
The true evaporation, as seeping is a kind of evaporating
The true evaporation, as the crack is too small to count
context: The class works out evaporation from the water each dish has lost, and the water that seeps through the crack is lost too, so that dish seems to have lost more to evaporation than it really did. Seeping is not evaporating: the water leaves through the crack as a liquid, not into the air as vapour, and even a slow seep adds up over a week. A leaky container is a source of error, and a scientist says which way it throws a result off before setting that result aside.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek scraped a little white matter, as thick as batter, from between his teeth in 1683. He mixed it with pure rainwater, and through his lens he saw many tiny living things moving about in it. What were they?
answer: Bacteria
choices: Bacteria
Viruses
Mites
Tiny worms
context: The tiny living things from his teeth were bacteria, and his letter of 17 September 1683 is often cited as the first clear sighting of them; his Dutch word for such creatures meant little animals, which his English translators turned into animalcules. The rainwater held none of them, so they had to come from his teeth. Viruses are far too small for any lens like his, and mites and worms are many-celled animals, far bigger than the single cells he saw.

question: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek wrote to the Royal Society in London in 1676 that one drop of pepper water held more than a million living creatures, all far too small for the eye. Some of the Fellows doubted him. What would give them the strongest evidence that he was right?
answer: A Fellow seeing them for himself through his own microscope
choices: A Fellow seeing them for himself through his own microscope
Eight respected men of Delft vouching that they saw them
Careful drawings of the creatures made by Leeuwenhoek
A longer letter from Leeuwenhoek counting them drop by drop
context: Witnesses, drawings and counts all depended on Leeuwenhoek and his own lenses, and he would not explain his methods; an observation that someone else repeats does not depend on him. The Society asked Robert Hooke to build a microscope strong enough, and in November 1677, after two failures, Hooke saw 'great numbers of exceedingly small animals swimming to and fro' before Christopher Wren and other Fellows. The minutes record that there was then no longer any doubt of Leeuwenhoek's discovery.

question: Plant cells stand out clearly under a microscope, each boxed in by a thick wall, and Matthias Schleiden argued in 1838 that every plant is built of them. Animal cells have no wall, so their edges are harder to see. Yet Theodor Schwann showed in 1839 that animals are built of cells too. What did he look for to pick out each cell?
answer: Its nucleus
choices: Its nucleus
Its chloroplasts
Its cytoplasm
Its mitochondria
context: Schleiden held the nucleus to be the most important part of a cell, and when the two men talked about nuclei, Schwann remembered seeing similar structures in animal cells; he reasoned that if plants and animals were built alike, the nucleus should turn up in animal tissue too, and his microscope found nuclei in tissue after tissue. Animal cells have no chloroplasts, the cytoplasm fills all the space around the nucleus and gives no single spot to look for, and mitochondria were not described until 1857.

question: Robert Remak watched red blood cells in chicken embryos split in two, and in 1852 he published his evidence that new cells come from cells that divide. Few took notice. Three years later another scientist made the idea famous in four Latin words meaning 'every cell from a cell', without naming Remak. Who was he?
answer: Rudolf Virchow
choices: Rudolf Virchow
Theodor Schwann
Matthias Schleiden
Louis Pasteur
context: Rudolf Virchow, a German doctor who had at first doubted that cells divide, made the Latin motto omnis cellula e cellula famous in 1855; his essay never named Remak, and the historian Paul Weindling says Virchow plagiarised Remak's idea. Schleiden and Schwann had thought that new cells form out of a fluid, as crystals do. Louis Pasteur's flasks of broth, a few years later, tested where microbes come from, not how cells are made.

question: A girl lays a thin slice of onion skin on a slide under her school microscope. So much light comes up through it that the pale cells look washed out and are hard to make out. Which part of the microscope should she adjust?
answer: The diaphragm
choices: The diaphragm
The fine focus knob
The eyepiece lens
The stage clips
context: The diaphragm, under the stage, opens and closes to let more or less light up through the slide, and closing it a little cuts the glare and makes pale cells stand out. The fine focus knob sharpens the picture, the eyepiece is the lens the eye looks through, and the stage clips only hold the slide in place.

question: A boy finds an onion cell with the low-power objective lens of his microscope, then turns the nosepiece to bring the high-power lens over the slide. Why should he now focus with only the fine focus knob, never the coarse one?
answer: The coarse knob could crash the lens into the slide
choices: The coarse knob could crash the lens into the slide
The coarse knob would change the lens's power again
The coarse knob moves the slide only from side to side
The coarse knob dims the light too much to see by
context: The coarse knob makes big moves, right for finding a cell at low power, but the high-power lens sits very close to the slide, and one big turn can scratch the lens and crack the slide. The fine knob makes the small moves high power needs. Focusing moves the lens and slide closer or farther apart and never changes the magnification.

question: A student's school microscope has an eyepiece lens marked 10x and a high-power objective lens, the one just above the slide, marked 40x. She looks at a slide of cheek cells with the high-power lens. How does she work out how many times bigger the cells look?
answer: Multiply the two numbers, 10 and 40
choices: Multiply the two numbers, 10 and 40
Add the two numbers, 10 and 40
Take the objective's number, 40, alone
Take the eyepiece's number, 10, alone
context: The objective makes a picture of the cells 40 times bigger, and the eyepiece enlarges that picture 10 times more, so the total magnification is the product of the two: 10 times 40 is 400. Adding the two would give only 50, and either number alone leaves out one of the two lenses the light passes through.

question: Ammonia is a colourless gas with a sharp smell, given off when bacteria and fungi break down rotting plants and animal waste. Its formula is NH3. What does each molecule of ammonia hold?
answer: One nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms
choices: One nitrogen atom and three hydrogen atoms
Three nitrogen atoms and three hydrogen atoms
Three nitrogen atoms and one hydrogen atom
One nitrogen atom and one hydrogen atom
context: A small number written after a symbol counts the atoms of that one element, and a symbol with no number stands for a single atom. So NH3 is one nitrogen atom joined to three hydrogen atoms: the 3 belongs to the hydrogen alone, not to the nitrogen before it.

question: Glucose is the sugar that the blood carries to the body's cells for energy, and its formula is C6H12O6. How many different elements does glucose hold?
answer: Three elements
choices: Three elements
Six elements
Twelve elements
Twenty-four elements
context: An element is one kind of atom, and glucose's formula holds three symbols: C for carbon, H for hydrogen and O for oxygen. The numbers count atoms, not elements: six carbon, twelve hydrogen and six oxygen, twenty-four atoms in all. Plants make glucose by photosynthesis.

question: Quartz, the mineral that most sand is made of, has the formula SiO2. Each grain of quartz sand is made of crystal, its silicon and oxygen atoms bonded together. What does the formula tell about a grain?
answer: It has two oxygen atoms for every silicon atom
choices: It has two oxygen atoms for every silicon atom
It has two silicon atoms for every oxygen atom
It has one silicon atom and two oxygen atoms in all
It has as many silicon atoms as oxygen atoms
context: In a crystal such as quartz, the atoms link into one network all through the crystal, so the formula gives a ratio: two oxygen atoms for every silicon atom, with countless atoms in a single grain. The 2 belongs to the oxygen alone.

question: The oxygen in air is a gas with no colour or smell, and its formula is O2. Ozone is a pale blue gas with a sharp smell that harms the lungs, and its formula is O3. What are oxygen gas and ozone?
answer: Two forms of one element
choices: Two forms of one element
An element and a compound
Two different elements
Two different compounds
context: An element is made of one kind of atom, and both gases hold nothing but oxygen atoms: two to a molecule in the oxygen people breathe, three in ozone. Joined atoms make a compound only when they belong to two or more different elements. High in the atmosphere, a layer of ozone absorbs nearly all of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light.

question: A drop of water can be split into smaller and smaller bits, but only so far: past a certain point, a bit is no longer water at all. What is the smallest bit that is still water?
answer: A single molecule of water
choices: A single molecule of water
A single atom of water
A single atom of oxygen
A single droplet, too small to see
context: A molecule is the smallest particle of a compound that keeps its makeup and chemical properties, and a water molecule is one oxygen atom joined to two hydrogen atoms. There is no such thing as a water atom: split a water molecule, and only hydrogen and oxygen are left, neither of them water. Even the tiniest droplet holds countless molecules.

question: Sodium is a soft metal that reacts violently with water, and chlorine is a poisonous yellow-green gas. Together they make sodium chloride, the table salt that the body needs. Why is the salt safe to eat when its elements are so dangerous?
answer: As a compound, it has properties all its own
choices: As a compound, it has properties all its own
Its properties are a blend, milder than either element's
It holds too little of each element to do harm
It is a mixture that keeps the two elements apart
context: Sodium chloride is a compound, a new substance with properties of its own: stable, unreactive and needed by the body in moderate amounts. It is not a blend of its elements' properties, and it is not a mixture, for its sodium and chlorine are joined one to one. Nor is it a weak dose of them: it is made of nothing but sodium and chlorine.

question: An electric current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, and each gas bubbles up into a tube of its own. The hydrogen always fills twice the space that the oxygen does. What explains the ratio?
answer: Water holds two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen
choices: Water holds two hydrogen atoms for each oxygen
A hydrogen atom is twice as big as an oxygen atom
Hydrogen is lighter, so it spreads to fill more space
Twice as much current flows to the hydrogen wire
context: Each water molecule holds two hydrogen atoms for every oxygen atom, so splitting water frees twice as much hydrogen. Both gases are made of two-atom molecules, and at the same temperature and pressure equal volumes of any gases hold equal numbers of molecules, however light or heavy the gas, so twice the hydrogen fills twice the space. A hydrogen atom is nowhere near twice the size of an oxygen atom, and the same current runs through both wires.

question: Joseph Proust, a French chemist, made copper carbonate in his laboratory and compared it with copper carbonate found in nature as a mineral. He measured how much of each element the two samples held. What did his measurements show about a compound?
answer: It holds its elements in fixed proportions
choices: It holds its elements in fixed proportions
It holds an equal mass of each element
Its proportions depend on how and where it formed
Its proportions slowly drift as the years pass
context: Proust found the same proportions by mass in both samples, about five parts copper to one of carbon and four of oxygen, however the copper carbonate had formed, and the same held for the other compounds he tested: a compound holds its elements in fixed proportions, though not equal ones. Claude Berthollet, another French chemist, argued that the proportions depend on how a compound forms, and the debate lasted years before the evidence settled it for Proust in the 1810s. A few crystals do vary slightly, and chemists call them berthollides after Berthollet.

question: John Dalton, an English chemist, set out his theory of atoms in a book of 1808. By his theory, what is true of the atoms in a bar of pure gold?
answer: They are all alike, with the same weight
choices: They are all alike, with the same weight
They can slowly turn into atoms of another metal
They are the same atoms every metal has
They are each yellow and shiny, like gold
context: Dalton held that each element has its own kind of atom, all alike and of the same weight, and that atoms are never created, destroyed or changed into another element's atoms. So pure gold holds gold atoms only, and lead, iron and every other metal are made of other kinds; the alchemists before him had thought metals formed in the earth from sulfur and mercury, and could be changed one into another. Later chemists found that the atoms of most elements come in a few slightly different weights, though gold's really are all alike. A single atom has no colour or shine: those belong to the metal, made of countless atoms together.

question: A science teacher lists four showy changes for her class to sort, and she warns them that a showy change is not always a chemical one. Which change makes a new substance?
answer: A firework bursting in the night sky
choices: A firework bursting in the night sky
Dry ice giving off a cold white fog
A balloon bursting with a loud pop
Iodine crystals warmed into a violet vapour
context: A firework's black powder burns in a flash into new substances: hot gases, mostly carbon dioxide and nitrogen, whose rush bursts the shell, and a white smoke of solid potassium salts. The balloon's rubber only tears, dry ice turns straight into carbon dioxide gas and iodine straight into iodine vapour, so none of those makes a new substance; the dry ice's fog is water from the air, condensed by the cold.

question: A glass beaker slips from a student's hand and shatters on the lab floor, and its pieces can never be fitted back into a beaker. Her lab partner says that a change that cannot be undone must be a chemical change. Why is he wrong?
answer: Each broken piece is still glass
choices: Each broken piece is still glass
Glass is far too hard a material to react
Glass is made from a mixture, and mixtures cannot react
Only a change giving off heat or light is chemical
context: A chemical change makes a new substance, and every shard is the same glass as before, so shattering is a physical change, however hard it is to undo; melted down, the pieces make glass again. Hardness decides nothing, since hydrofluoric acid etches hard glass. Mixtures can react, as iron and sulfur powders do when heated together, and many chemical changes, such as a nail rusting, give off no light.

question: A silver cup stands for years in a museum case, and slowly a thin black film of tarnish grows over it. What is the black film?
answer: Silver joined with sulfur from the air
choices: Silver joined with sulfur from the air
Silver joined with oxygen from the air
Fine dust from the air, settled on the silver
Silver darkened by age, still pure silver
context: Traces of sulfur gases in the air, such as hydrogen sulfide given off by wool and rubber, react with the silver and make black silver sulfide, a new substance, so tarnishing is a chemical change. The tarnish on silver holds no oxygen at all. Each polishing rubs away a little of the silver along with the film, since the film is partly made of it.

question: Michael Faraday lectured to young people at the Royal Institution in London on the chemistry of a candle. He blew a candle out and held a flame in the vapour rising from its wick, and fire ran down through the air and lit the candle again. What was the vapour?
answer: Wax turned into a gas
choices: Wax turned into a gas
Steam made by the burning wax
Carbon dioxide from the flame
Air heated by the flame
context: The flame melts the wax, the liquid climbs the wick, and the heat turns it into a gas: changes of state that leave it wax, still able to burn. Only the burning in the flame is a chemical change, and it makes carbon dioxide and water vapour, which cannot burn. Air is no fuel either, so only the wax vapour could carry the fire back to the wick.

question: A student strikes a match and lets it burn until only a thin black stick is left. Nothing she does to that stick will ever make it fresh wood again. Why not?
answer: The wood has become new substances
choices: The wood has become new substances
The wood's particles have shrunk in the heat
The wood's shape has changed too far to undo
The wood is coated in soot that will not wash off
context: Burning turns the wood's substances into carbon dioxide, water vapour and ash, and the black stick left is charcoal, mostly carbon, so no change of shape or size could ever make it wood again. Particles do not shrink when they are heated, and the stick is charcoal itself, not wood under a coat of soot.

question: A teacher touches the ends of a 9-volt battery to a pad of fine steel wool, which is mostly iron. The wool glows and burns with sparks, leaving a dark, brittle mass. How is this burning like the slow rusting of an iron nail left out in the rain?
answer: Both join iron with oxygen from the air
choices: Both join iron with oxygen from the air
Both join iron with nitrogen from the air
Both turn iron into a different form of iron
Both break iron into tiny bits of iron
context: In both, iron joins with oxygen from the air and becomes iron oxide, a new substance, so both are chemical changes: the dark mass and the rust are no longer iron at all. The thin wool reacts in seconds and needs no water, while the nail takes months and rusts only where it is wet. Nitrogen from the air takes no part in either.

question: A granite boulder sits out through many years of sun, wind, rain and frost, and its hard feldspar crystals slowly turn into a soft, white clay that can be moulded when wet. What is the clay?
answer: Feldspar made into a new mineral by rain
choices: Feldspar made into a new mineral by rain
Feldspar split fine by ice in its cracks
Feldspar worn to dust by wind-blown sand
Feldspar crumbled by daily heating and cooling
context: Rainwater, made a weak acid by carbon dioxide from the air, reacts with the feldspar and turns it into kaolinite, a clay mineral with new properties, so this is chemical weathering. Ice in cracks, wind-blown sand and daily heating and cooling only break rock into smaller pieces of the same minerals: physical weathering. Quartz, another of granite's minerals, resists this weathering.

question: A student strokes a large iron nail again and again in one direction with a strong magnet. Afterward the nail picks up paper clips on its own, which it could not do before. Has the nail gone through a chemical change?
answer: No, the nail is still the same iron
choices: No, the nail is still the same iron
Yes, it has gained a property it lacked
Yes, its iron has joined with the magnet's
No, a chemical change needs heat or a flame
context: Stroking lines up tiny groups of the iron's atoms, called domains, so that their magnetism points one way, but no new substance forms: the nail is still iron, so magnetizing it is a physical change. A new property alone does not make a new substance, and the nail's iron does not join with the magnet's. Many chemical changes, such as rusting, need no heat or flame at all.

question: Inside an old-style light bulb, a thin wire of the metal tungsten glows white-hot whenever the bulb is switched on, giving off light and a great deal of heat. Is the glowing wire going through a chemical change?
answer: No, the wire stays tungsten all along
choices: No, the wire stays tungsten all along
Yes, it gives off light and heat
Yes, the tungsten burns in the air inside the bulb
No, electricity cannot cause a chemical change
context: Light and heat are only clues: the current heats the wire until it glows, and it is still tungsten when it cools, so the glow is a physical change. The bulb holds no air, only a vacuum or an unreactive gas, so the wire cannot burn. Electricity can drive chemical changes, as when a current splits water into hydrogen and oxygen, but here it only heats the wire, which slowly thins as tungsten atoms escape from it as a gas.

question: Bronze is a hard metal made of about 88 parts copper to 12 parts tin, melted together and cooled into one evenly mixed solid. Chemists count it as a solution. Which part is the solvent, and why?
answer: Copper, as there is more of it
choices: Copper, as there is more of it
Tin, as there is less of it
Tin, as it makes the copper harder
Tin, as it is spread all through the copper
context: The solvent is the part a solution holds the most of, and the solute is the part spread through it, so in bronze the copper is the solvent and the tin a solute dissolved in it. Tin does make bronze harder than pure copper, but that does not decide which part is the solvent. A solution need not be a liquid: brass and sterling silver are solid solutions too, and chemists call such solutions alloys.

question: When the tide goes out, a rock pool is left cut off from the sea, full of ordinary seawater. All through a hot, sunny afternoon, much of the water in the pool evaporates. What happens to the concentration of salt in the pool?
answer: It rises, as the same salt is in less water
choices: It rises, as the same salt is in less water
It falls, as the salt goes off with the water
It stays the same, as no salt has been added
It falls, as less salt water is left in the pool
context: Concentration is how much solute a given amount of solution holds. Evaporation takes away only water, so the salt left behind is crowded into less of it: seawater holds about 35 grams of salt in each kilogram, and a sun-baked rock pool can reach 50 or more. Rain does the opposite, diluting the pool with fresh water.

question: A geologist drops a walnut-sized lump of rock salt, the mineral halite, into a large beaker of water. Into a second beaker of the same water she drops the same mass of rock salt, crushed to small grains. Neither beaker is stirred. Which salt is gone first, and why?
answer: The grains, as more of their surface meets the water
choices: The grains, as more of their surface meets the water
The grains, as small bits of salt are softer than a lump
Both at once, as each holds the same mass of salt
The lump, as water seeps deep into its many cracks
context: Water can only work on a solid where it touches it. Crushing the lump bares far more surface to the water, so the grains dissolve much faster; the lump holds the same mass of salt, but most of it is hidden inside, away from the water.

question: A student drops a blue crystal of copper sulfate into a beaker of cold water and an identical crystal into a beaker of hot water. She stirs neither one. The crystal in the hot water is gone long before the other. Why does the hotter water dissolve it faster?
answer: Its particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
choices: Its particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
Its heat melts the crystal into a blue liquid first
Its heat turns the crystal into a new substance
Its particles grow bigger and push the crystal apart
context: Heating water gives its particles more energy, so they move faster, strike the crystal more often and carry its particles off sooner. The crystal dissolves rather than melts, no new substance forms, and the water's particles stay the same size however hot it gets.

question: A student pours equal scoops of Epsom salt, the crystals used in soaks for sore muscles, into two beakers of warm water. She stirs one beaker and leaves the other still, and the stirred salt is gone far sooner. Why does stirring speed up the dissolving?
answer: It keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
choices: It keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
It splits the salt's particles into smaller bits
It lets the water hold more of the salt in all
It helps the salt react with the water sooner
context: The water right next to a crystal soon fills with dissolved salt and takes in more only slowly; stirring sweeps it away and brings fresh water up against the crystal. Stirring changes how fast the salt dissolves, not how much the water can hold, no particle is split, and dissolving makes no new substance, so nothing reacts.

question: A student stirs spoonful after spoonful of potassium nitrate, a white salt, into a beaker of water at room temperature. At last some crystals stay on the bottom, because the solution is saturated. Which change will get more of those crystals to dissolve?
answer: Warming the water in the beaker
choices: Warming the water in the beaker
Stirring the water much faster
Crushing the crystals to a powder
Leaving the beaker to stand for days
context: A saturated solution holds all the solute it can at its temperature, and stirring, crushing or waiting only make a solid dissolve faster, never make room for more. Warmer water holds more of most solids, and potassium nitrate is a strong case: water near boiling holds more than seven times as much as water at 20 degrees Celsius.

question: Oxygen gas is dissolved in the water of a pond. Over a long, hot summer the pond warms from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. How does the amount of oxygen its water can hold change?
answer: It falls, as warm water holds less gas
choices: It falls, as warm water holds less gas
It rises, as warm water dissolves more
It stays the same, as only solids change
It stays the same, as the air above it has not changed
context: Unlike most solids, gases dissolve less in warmer water, because heat helps their particles escape it: fresh water at 20 degrees Celsius can hold about 9 milligrams of oxygen in a litre, but at 30 degrees only about 7.6. That is why hot, calm summer weather can leave pond fish short of oxygen, while cold, tumbling streams hold plenty.

question: A sealed bottle of fizzy water stands on a shelf, and no bubbles can be seen in it. When its cap is twisted off, bubbles stream up through the water. Why do the bubbles appear only now?
answer: Less gas can stay dissolved once the pressure drops
choices: Less gas can stay dissolved once the pressure drops
The water starts to boil as the pressure drops
Air rushes in and forms bubbles all through the water
Air rushes in and reacts with the water to make a gas
context: At the bottling plant, carbon dioxide is forced into chilled water under pressure and the tight cap keeps the pressure in, and the more pressure a gas is under, the more of it a liquid can hold. Opening the bottle drops the pressure to that of ordinary air, so the carbon dioxide the water can no longer keep comes out as bubbles. The bubbles are carbon dioxide, not air, and the water is far too cool to boil.

question: A girl cycles to her grandmother's house. Whenever she is moving, her bike's speedometer reads 20 kilometres per hour, but halfway there she stops for a half-hour rest. How does her average speed for the whole trip compare with 20 kilometres per hour?
answer: Lower, since the rest adds time but no distance
choices: Lower, since the rest adds time but no distance
Lower, since the rest shortens the distance ridden
The same, since stops are left out of an average
The same, since she always rides at that speed
context: Average speed is the total distance divided by the total time, and the half hour of rest counts in the time. The road to her grandmother's house is just as long either way, so the rest pulls her average below the 20 kilometres per hour her speedometer showed while she rode.

question: A radio weather report says only that a storm is moving at 30 kilometres per hour. A science teacher listening points out that the report has given the storm's speed, but not its velocity. What has the report left out?
answer: Which way the storm is heading
choices: Which way the storm is heading
How long the storm has been moving
How far the storm has travelled
Whether the storm is speeding up
context: Velocity is speed with a direction, so 30 kilometres per hour toward the east is a velocity. For a town nearby, the direction decides whether the storm arrives at all. How long it has moved and how far it has come are not part of velocity, and a change of speed is acceleration.

question: Mia and Ben cycle away from the same gate at the same moment. On a distance-time graph, with distance up the side and time along the bottom, each ride makes a straight line, and Mia's rises more steeply than Ben's. What does the graph show?
answer: Mia rides faster than Ben
choices: Mia rides faster than Ben
Mia rides more slowly than Ben
Mia rides up a steeper hill
Mia speeds up while Ben holds steady
context: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed: a steeper line gains more distance each second, so Mia is faster. The graph shows distance against time, not the shape of the road, and a straight line means each rider holds one steady speed.

question: A boy walks from his house to a shop. On the distance-time graph of his trip, the line rises, then runs flat for five minutes, then rises again until he reaches the shop. What was he doing during the flat part?
answer: Standing still in one spot
choices: Standing still in one spot
Walking at one steady speed
Walking along level ground
Walking back toward his house
context: A flat line on a distance-time graph means time passes while the distance stays the same, so he was not moving. A flat line means a steady speed only on a speed-time graph, and a distance-time graph shows nothing about whether the ground is level.

question: A tram's distance-time graph for one minute of its run starts as a steep line, then keeps rising, but less and less steeply as the minute goes on. What does the graph show about the tram?
answer: It is slowing down
choices: It is slowing down
It is speeding up
It holds one steady speed
It is coming over a hill
context: The slope of a distance-time graph is the speed, so a line growing less steep shows the tram covering less distance each second. The line still rises because the tram is still moving forward, and its bend shows how the speed changes, not the shape of the ground.

question: Two sisters race down a straight track, and the younger is given a 10-metre head start. On a graph of distance from the start line against time, each girl's run makes a straight line, and partway through the race the two lines cross. What does the crossing point show about the sisters?
answer: They are side by side on the track
choices: They are side by side on the track
They are running at the same speed
The younger sister is pulling ahead
They are swapping lanes on the track
context: Where the lines cross, both sisters are the same distance from the start line at the same moment, so they are side by side. Their speeds are the slopes, and lines that cross have different slopes: the older sister's steeper line shows she has made up the 10 metres and is passing the younger. The graph shows distance against time, not the lanes they run in.

question: A racing car takes a long, sweeping curve of its track at a steady 200 kilometres per hour, and its speed reading never changes all the way round. Is the car accelerating on the curve?
answer: Yes, since its direction changes
choices: Yes, since its direction changes
Yes, since it is moving very fast
No, since its speed stays the same
No, since only speeding up counts
context: Acceleration is any change in velocity, and velocity includes direction, so a car rounding a curve at a steady speed accelerates all the way round. In everyday speech to accelerate means to speed up, but in science a change of direction counts too. Going fast is not the same thing: the same car holding 200 kilometres per hour on a straight is not accelerating at all.

question: A bus driver sees the next stop ahead and presses the brake. Along the straight street, the bus slows steadily from 40 to 10 kilometres per hour. Is the bus accelerating while it slows?
answer: Yes, since its speed is changing
choices: Yes, since its speed is changing
No, since it is slowing down
No, since it is not turning
Yes, since it is still moving forward
context: Acceleration is any change in velocity, so a bus that slows down is accelerating, with its acceleration pointing backward, against its motion. Everyday speech calls this deceleration, but in science it counts as acceleration. Moving is not enough on its own: a bus holding one speed along a straight street is not accelerating.

question: Galileo Galilei timed bronze balls rolling down grooves cut in wooden ramps. He reasoned that a ball rolling down one ramp and up a second one climbs almost back to its starting height, however steep the second ramp is. Then he asked what the ball would do if the second ramp were laid flat and perfectly smooth. What did he conclude?
answer: It would roll on forever at the same speed
choices: It would roll on forever at the same speed
It would slow down with no slope to push it
It would stop as soon as it reached the flat
It would keep speeding up along the flat
context: On a flat second ramp the ball could never climb back to its starting height, so Galileo concluded that it would roll on and on without slowing: nothing is needed to keep a moving thing moving. Real balls stop because friction and the air push against them, which is why a ball rolled across grass stops far sooner than one on smooth ice. Aristotle had taught that a pushed thing stops once nothing pushes it, and many people still picture a push that slowly wears off.

question: A space probe far out between the stars, with no star or planet anywhere near it, shuts off its engines. By Newton's first law, the law of inertia, what happens to its motion after that?
answer: It keeps moving straight on at the same speed
choices: It keeps moving straight on at the same speed
It keeps going, but slower and slower until it stops
It stops at once, with no engine to push it
It keeps its speed, but curves round in a slow circle
context: With almost no force acting on it, the probe goes on in a straight line at the same speed, as Newton's first law says. It would take a force, such as a rocket firing or a planet's pull nearby, to speed it up, slow it down or bend its path. On Earth moving things stop because friction and the air push against them, but out between the stars there is nothing to rub against.

question: Aboard a space station in orbit, a big cardboard box stuffed with foam and a small steel toolbox crammed with tools float side by side. A bathroom scale would read nothing for either of them. An astronaut gives each a shove to send it drifting across the cabin. Which one is harder to set moving?
answer: The toolbox, since it has more mass
choices: The toolbox, since it has more mass
The foam box, since it is bigger
Neither, since neither has any weight
Neither, since nothing rubs against them
context: A scale reads nothing for either, but neither has lost any mass, and mass, the amount of matter in a thing, is what gives it inertia. The small toolbox holds far more matter than the big box of foam, so it is far harder to start; size does not count, and with no floor to slide on, friction plays no part. A NASA lesson makes the same point with an astronaut struggling to push a one-ton satellite out of a space shuttle's cargo bay.

question: A driver slams on the brakes, and her car jolts to a stop. Her passenger, who has not buckled his seat belt, lurches forward toward the dashboard. Why does he lurch forward?
answer: His body goes on moving as the car stops
choices: His body goes on moving as the car stops
The braking car throws him forward
The seat behind him pushes him forward
A force stored up from the drive carries him on
context: He was moving at the car's speed, and the brakes slow only the car, so his body goes on moving until something stops it: the dashboard or the windshield, if he is not buckled in. A seat belt gives the force that slows him along with the car, spread across the strong bones of the hips and shoulder. Nothing throws him forward and no stored-up force carries him on; the car simply stops beneath him.

question: A car swings left around a sharp bend at a steady speed. A box of apples on the back seat slides across to the right and bumps against the right-hand door. Why does the box slide to the right?
answer: It goes on straight while the car turns
choices: It goes on straight while the car turns
An outward force flings it away from the bend
Its weight pulls it to the outside of the bend
The turning car pushes it toward the door
context: The box keeps moving in a straight line while the car turns left beneath it, so the right-hand door swings round to meet it; the seat's grip is too weak to turn the box with the car. Passengers feel flung outward on a bend for the same reason, and the outward force they seem to feel is not a real push from anything.

question: A magician sets plates and glasses on a smooth silk cloth. He yanks the cloth sharply away, and the dishes are left standing on the bare table. Why does the sharp yank leave them in place?
answer: Friction has too little time to move them
choices: Friction has too little time to move them
A fast-moving cloth has no friction at all
Inertia grips the dishes down onto the table
The yank flicks the dishes up off the cloth
context: The cloth rubs on the dishes all the while it slides, but a sharp yank is over so fast that friction acts for too short a time to get them moving much, and their inertia keeps them almost where they were. A slow tug gives friction time to drag them off with the cloth. Inertia is not a grip that holds things down; it is only their resistance to a change in motion.

question: A girl whirls a ball on a string in a flat circle above her head. Partway round, the string snaps. Seen from directly above, what path does the ball take as it flies away?
answer: A straight line, the way it was heading
choices: A straight line, the way it was heading
A curve that keeps bending round and round
A straight line directly out away from her
A spiral that slowly widens out from her
context: The string's pull was all that bent the ball's path into a circle, so once it snaps the ball goes on in a straight line in the direction it was moving at that instant, along the edge of the circle. In studies in the 1980s, many college students expected a ball let go from a curved path to keep curving, an idea much like the old theory of impetus.

question: A boy sits on a train gliding along a straight, level track at a steady speed. He tosses a ball straight up above his lap, and while it is in the air the train rolls on down the track. Where does the ball come down?
answer: Back down into his hand
choices: Back down into his hand
A little way behind him
A little way ahead of him
Behind him, as far as the train has gone
context: The ball was already moving forward with the train when it left his hand, and nothing pushes it backward, so it keeps the train's speed and stays above his hand all the way up and down. Galileo argued the same in his Dialogue of 1632 about a stone dropped from the top of a smoothly sailing ship's mast: it falls at the foot of the mast, not behind it.

question: A student heats a brass weight in a beaker of boiling water, then drops it into a cup of cool water. A thermometer in the cup climbs for a while, then stops climbing. What is true once the thermometer stops?
answer: The weight and the water share one temperature
choices: The weight and the water share one temperature
The weight is as cool as the water was at first
The water is as hot as the boiling water was
The weight has no heat left in it at all
context: Heat flows from the hot weight into the cool water until the two reach the same temperature, somewhere between where each began, and then the flow stops. The weight is still warm at that point; what has gone is the difference in temperature that drove the flow.

question: A coach props a player's swollen ankle up on an ice pack, so the pack lies underneath the ankle instead of on top of it. Does heat flow out of the ankle down into the pack?
answer: Yes, heat flows into the cold pack below it
choices: Yes, heat flows into the cold pack below it
No, heat only rises, so it cannot flow down
Only a little, as heat flows mostly upward
No, the pack's cold sinks away from the ankle
context: Heat passes by conduction from a warmer thing to a cooler one it touches, in any direction, so it flows down out of the ankle into the pack as readily as into a pack laid on top. The saying that heat rises is a mix-up: what rises is warm air, not heat.

question: A metal spoon stands in a beaker of hot water. After a minute or two, the top of its handle, well above the water, feels warm to the touch. How does the heat travel up the spoon's handle?
answer: Particles bump their neighbours, passing energy on
choices: Particles bump their neighbours, passing energy on
An invisible heat fluid seeps up through the metal
The hottest metal slowly creeps up toward the top
Rays of heat shine up along the inside of the metal
context: This is conduction: particles at the hot end jiggle faster and bump into the ones beside them, passing energy along, while the metal itself stays put. Many scientists of the late 1700s explained heat as an invisible fluid they called caloric, but experiments showed heat is energy on the move, and the idea was given up in the 1800s.

question: A student lets a crystal of potassium permanganate, which colours water purple, sink to the bottom of a beaker of water near one side. Then she heats the base of the beaker gently, just under the crystal. Which way does the purple colour travel?
answer: Up the heated side, across the top, down the far side
choices: Up the heated side, across the top, down the far side
Up the far side, across the top, down the heated side
Straight up the heated side, then it stays at the top
Out evenly in every direction from the crystal
context: Water warmed at the bottom grows less dense and rises, carrying the purple up the heated side; at the top it moves across, cools, grows denser and sinks down the far side. This loop is a convection current, and the moving water carries the heat with it.

question: Heat moves by conduction, convection and radiation, and often by more than one of them at once. Four things are warming up. In which case is most of the heat carried by convection?
answer: A hot-water radiator warming a chilly classroom
choices: A hot-water radiator warming a chilly classroom
A hot-water bottle warming a child's cold feet
Sunlight warming a car's seats through its windows
A sun-baked stone wall warming a hand laid on it
context: Despite its name, a typical radiator gives off only about a quarter of its heat as radiation; mostly it warms the air touching it, and that air rises and flows round the room in a convection current. The hot-water bottle and the wall warm by touch, which is conduction, and sunlight through glass is radiation.

question: Campers sit in a ring round a campfire on a cold night, a few steps back from the flames, and soon their faces feel warm. How does most of the fire's heat reach their faces?
answer: As rays that spread straight out from the flames
choices: As rays that spread straight out from the flames
In warm air that flows straight out from the flames
Through the air, passed on from particle to particle
As heat that rises, then spreads down onto them
context: Most of the warmth a camper feels beside a fire is thermal radiation, mostly infrared rays that travel out in straight lines in every direction. The fire's hot air does carry heat by convection, but it rises straight up into the sky, and air is such a poor conductor that little heat crosses it particle to particle.

question: Builders lay thick mats of fibreglass, a loose tangle of very thin glass threads, in the attic of a house. A slab of solid glass as thick as a mat would let far more heat through, yet the mats help keep the house warm in winter. Why do they slow heat so well?
answer: They trap air in pockets too small for it to flow
choices: They trap air in pockets too small for it to flow
Their glass threads soak up heat and store it
Their glass threads are hollow, with a vacuum inside
Glass spun into thin threads cannot carry heat
context: Still air is a poor conductor, and the tangle of threads breaks it into tiny pockets where it cannot flow round in convection currents. The solid glass threads still conduct a little heat, but there is so little glass and so much trapped air that heat creeps through slowly.

question: A vacuum flask has two glass walls, one inside the other, and the air has been pumped out of the narrow gap between them. With almost nothing left in the gap, which ways of moving heat can barely cross it?
answer: Conduction and convection
choices: Conduction and convection
Conduction and radiation
Convection and radiation
Conduction, convection and radiation
context: Conduction needs particles to bump into one another, and convection needs a liquid or gas to flow, so a near-empty gap blocks them both. Radiation needs no matter at all, which is how sunlight crosses empty space to Earth, so the walls facing the gap are silvered like a mirror to reflect it back.

question: At the finish line of a marathon, helpers wrap tired runners in space blankets: thin plastic sheets coated with a very thin layer of aluminium. A runner's warm body gives off heat all the time. How does the metal coating help him keep that heat?
answer: Its metal reflects his heat rays back to him
choices: Its metal reflects his heat rays back to him
Its metal soaks up his heat rays and holds them
Its metal spreads his heat evenly over his body
Its metal is a poor conductor that holds heat in
context: Every warm body radiates infrared heat, and the thin aluminium layer reflects up to 97 percent of it back toward the runner, since shiny metal absorbs very little. Aluminium is a good conductor of heat, not a poor one. The plastic sheet also blocks the wind and holds in moisture, which cuts the heat lost by convection and evaporation.

question: Two beakers of water stand side by side on a lab bench, and the thermometers in both read 60 degrees Celsius. One beaker is full to the brim; the other holds only a few spoonfuls of water. How does the average speed of the water particles compare in the two beakers?
answer: The same in both
choices: The same in both
Faster in the full one
Faster in the few spoonfuls
Faster in whichever was heated longer
context: A thermometer reads the average energy of motion of the water's particles, and at 60 degrees that average, and with it the particles' average speed, is the same however much water there is. How long either beaker was heated makes no difference once both read the same.

question: A kettle has just filled a mug with boiling water. Down the hall stands a bathtub full of warm bath water, far cooler than the water in the mug. Which of the two holds more thermal energy?
answer: The bathtub, since it holds far more water
choices: The bathtub, since it holds far more water
The mug, since its water is much hotter
The bathtub, since its particles move faster
Both the same, since both are plain water
context: Thermal energy is the energy of motion of all of a thing's particles added together. The mug's particles move faster on average, which is why its temperature is higher, but the bathtub holds so many more particles that their energy adds up to far more: temperature is an average, thermal energy a total.

question: A student heats a beaker of crushed ice over a low flame, stirring as it melts, with a thermometer in the ice. The reading stays at 0 degrees Celsius for many minutes until the last of the ice has melted, and only then starts to climb. While the reading holds steady, where does the flame's energy go?
answer: Into freeing particles, not speeding them up
choices: Into freeing particles, not speeding them up
Into speeding particles up, not freeing them
Into the beaker's glass, not into the ice
Into swelling the particles, not moving them
context: While the ice melts, the energy that flows in breaks particles free of the fixed places that hold them in the solid, so their average speed, and with it the temperature, stays the same. Once all the ice is liquid, the energy speeds the particles up again and the reading rises.

question: A brass ball just slips through a brass ring when both are cool. A teacher heats only the ball in a gas flame, and now it rests on top of the ring and will not pass through. What has changed inside the hot ball?
answer: Its particles sit a little farther apart
choices: Its particles sit a little farther apart
Each of its particles has grown a little larger
A fluid of heat has filled the gaps between them
Particles from the flame have joined its own
context: Heating makes the ball's particles jiggle harder, and as they jostle they push one another a little farther apart, so the whole ball grows; the particles themselves stay the same size. Many scientists of the late 1700s thought a heat fluid called caloric seeped in between the particles and pushed them apart, but the idea was given up in the 1800s, once heat was shown to be energy.

question: Where a long concrete bridge meets the road at each end, a gap runs across the roadway, spanned by interlocking steel teeth. An engineer measures one gap on a cold winter morning and again on a hot summer afternoon. How does the summer gap compare with the winter one?
answer: Narrower, since the bridge has grown longer
choices: Narrower, since the bridge has grown longer
Wider, since the bridge has grown shorter
Wider, since the gap itself grows in the heat
The same, since concrete is too hard to grow
context: In summer heat the bridge expands, so its ends push into the gaps and narrow them; in winter the concrete contracts and the gaps open wide again. These expansion joints let a bridge change length without buckling, and railways laid in separate lengths leave small gaps between their rails for the same reason.

question: A lab technician cannot twist the metal lid off a glass jar of samples. She holds the lid under a stream of hot water for a minute, and then it turns easily. Why does the lid loosen?
answer: The metal lid expands more than the glass
choices: The metal lid expands more than the glass
The glass expands more than the metal lid
The heat makes the jar's glass rim shrink
The hot water makes the metal lid softer
context: Metal expands more than glass for the same warming, and the hot water heats the lid faster than the glass beneath it, so the lid grows a little wider than the rim and its grip loosens. Glass expands when heated too, only less, and a metal lid stays hard far above the temperature of hot water.

question: Galileo Galilei made an early thermoscope in Padua. A glass bulb the size of a hen's egg had a long, thin neck, and he turned it upside down so that the neck's open end dipped into a bowl of water. Water stood partway up the neck, with air trapped in the bulb above it. When the room grew warmer, what did the water in the neck do?
answer: It sank lower, pushed down by the expanding air
choices: It sank lower, pushed down by the expanding air
It rose higher, drawn up by the warming air
It rose higher, as the warmed water expanded
It stayed put, as the glass kept the heat out
context: Warmed air expands far more than water does, so the air in the bulb pushed the water down the neck, and when it cooled the water rose again: Galileo's device ran the opposite way to a modern thermometer. In a liquid-in-glass thermometer the liquid itself expands more than its glass and climbs the tube.

question: Two thermometers hang side by side in a weather station's shelter, in moving air. One has its bulb wrapped in a cloth kept wet with water, and it reads several degrees lower than the dry one. Why is the wet bulb colder?
answer: The fastest water particles escape, carrying energy off
choices: The fastest water particles escape, carrying energy off
The slowest water particles escape, leaving the fast ones
The water particles give off cold into the bulb
The water particles shield the bulb from the heat
context: The particles of a liquid move at many speeds, and only the fastest at the surface can break free into the air, so the water left behind is slower on average and colder, and it draws heat from the bulb. Cold is not a thing that flows into the bulb, and the low reading is a real temperature: weather observers compare the two thermometers to measure the air's humidity.

question: In their laboratories, physicists have chilled atoms to less than a billionth of a degree above absolute zero, yet nothing anywhere can ever be colder than absolute zero itself. What makes absolute zero the coldest temperature there can be?
answer: Particles there have the least energy possible
choices: Particles there have the least energy possible
Particles there are all locked in solids
No thermometer can read any lower
Scientists agreed to end the scale there
context: Cooling takes energy from particles and slows them, and at absolute zero they would have the least energy they can possibly have, with nothing more to take away; even then a tiny quantum jiggle remains. Helium never freezes at ordinary pressure, even at absolute zero, and the zero is set by nature, not by choice: Guillaume Amontons estimated it in 1703 from the way air presses less as it cools.

question: A blacksmith has hammered iron at his forge for twenty years, and his arms have grown thick and strong from the work. Later he has a son. How much of the strength the blacksmith built at the forge does the boy inherit through his genes?
answer: None of it
choices: None of it
About a quarter of it
About half of it
All of it
context: Strength built by work is an acquired trait: it changes the blacksmith's muscles, not the genes he passes on, so none of it is inherited. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, a French naturalist, taught that traits gained by use pass to the young, but genetics found no way for that to happen. A child gets about half of his or her genes from each parent, but that half rule is about genes, not about what a parent gains in life.

question: Gregor Mendel was a monk at St Thomas's Abbey in Brno, and he grew peas in its garden. He crossed a kind of pea that always grew tall with a kind that always grew short, then planted the seeds of the cross. How did that first generation of offspring grow?
answer: All of them tall
choices: All of them tall
All of them medium height
Half tall and half short
Mostly tall, with a few short
context: Every plant of the first generation grew tall, and the short trait seemed to have vanished. Most naturalists of the day expected blending, offspring halfway between their parents, and Mendel's peas showed nothing of the kind. He called the trait that showed in every hybrid dominant.

question: Gregor Mendel took the hybrid peas from his cross of tall plants with short ones and let them pollinate themselves. Then he grew their seeds and counted the plants of this second generation. How did they come out?
answer: About three tall for every short one
choices: About three tall for every short one
About one tall for every short one
All tall, with no short ones at all
All of a height between the two
context: He counted 787 tall plants and 277 short ones, close to three to one, so about one plant in four was short again. The short trait had hidden for a generation and come back as short as ever. Mendel called a trait that hides like this recessive.

question: To explain his peas, Gregor Mendel proposed hereditary factors, later named genes, that pass from parents to offspring. A hybrid pea gets a factor for tall from one parent and a factor for short from the other. By Mendel's account, what becomes of the two factors inside it?
answer: They stay separate and unchanged
choices: They stay separate and unchanged
They blend into one in-between factor
The short one is used up and lost
The tall one turns the short one tall
context: Mendel's factors were separate units that never mixed, so a tall hybrid could pass its short factor on as whole as it came in. That is why short plants could appear again a generation later, which blending, the idea that parents' traits fuse like mixed paints, could not explain. Wilhelm Johannsen, a Danish botanist, named the factors genes in 1909.

question: A pea plant carries two copies of the gene for stem height. The versions of a gene are called alleles, and this plant has one tall allele and one short allele. When it makes pollen, what does each grain of pollen carry?
answer: One allele, tall or short by chance
choices: One allele, tall or short by chance
Both alleles, the tall and the short
One allele, always the dominant one
A new allele, blended from the two
context: Each grain of pollen, and each egg cell, gets just one of the plant's two alleles, and either one is equally likely. A seed then holds two again, one from each parent. If only the dominant allele were passed on, a short plant could never come from a tall hybrid.

question: In pea plants, tall is dominant over short, and every plant carries two copies of the gene for height. A grower crosses two tall plants, and one of their seeds grows into a short plant. What must be true of the two tall parents?
answer: Each carries one short copy
choices: Each carries one short copy
Only one carries a short copy
Each carries two short copies
Neither carries a short copy
context: A recessive trait shows only when an offspring gets the recessive copy from both parents, so each tall parent passed a short copy to that seed. Each parent still grew tall because one tall copy is enough to make a plant tall. A plant with two short copies would itself be short.

question: In peas, tall is dominant over short. A pea plant with one tall copy and one short copy of the height gene is crossed with a short plant. A Punnett square, a grid that pairs up each parent's possible copies, gives the chances for their seeds. About what share of the seeds should grow into short plants?
answer: About one half
choices: About one half
About one in four
About three in four
None at all
context: The short parent has only short copies to pass on, while the hybrid passes tall or short with equal chance. Two of the square's four boxes get two short copies, so about half the seeds should grow short. One in four is the share when two hybrids are crossed, and even then the square gives only the chances, not an exact count.

question: In peas, tall is dominant over short. One pea plant carries two tall alleles, or versions, of the height gene. A second carries one tall allele and one short allele. How do the two plants compare?
answer: Same phenotype, different genotype
choices: Same phenotype, different genotype
Same genotype, different phenotype
Same genotype and same phenotype
Different genotype and phenotype
context: A genotype is the pair of alleles a living thing carries, and a phenotype is the trait that shows. One tall allele is enough to make a pea tall, so both plants grow tall and share a phenotype, but their genotypes differ. Wilhelm Johannsen, a Danish botanist, coined both words in 1909.

question: Gregor Mendel read his pea results to the Natural History Society of Brno in 1865, and the society printed his paper the next year. What became of the paper over the next thirty years?
answer: Few scientists took any notice of it
choices: Few scientists took any notice of it
Charles Darwin built it into his theory
Botanists repeated it and proved it wrong
It made Mendel famous in his lifetime
context: The paper sat in a small society's journal and was cited only a handful of times before 1900; Charles Darwin, whose own idea of heredity was pangenesis, seems never to have known of it.
