context: The strong force pulls on protons and neutrons alike, about a hundred times harder than the electric push between two protons that close, but it fades to almost nothing beyond about two and a half trillionths of a millimetre, so each particle grips only its nearest neighbours and never reaches the next atom; electrons do not feel it at all. That is why a big nucleus such as uranium's is fragile: every proton pushes on every other proton, but grips only those beside it.

question: Between two protons, the pull of gravity is about a trillion trillion trillion times weaker than their electric push, and of the four fundamental forces, gravity is by far the weakest. Yet it is gravity, not the electric force, that holds the Moon on its path round Earth and Earth on its path round the Sun. Why does the weakest force win at that scale?
answer: Mass only attracts, but plus and minus charges cancel out
choices: Mass only attracts, but plus and minus charges cancel out
The electric force fades with distance far faster than gravity
The electric force cannot travel across empty space
The Moon and Earth hold no charged particles at all
context: Gravity only ever pulls, so the pull of every atom in Earth and the Moon adds up, while each holds almost exactly as much negative charge as positive, so its electric pushes and pulls cancel. Both forces fade with distance in the same way, and both reach across space without end. The other two forces, the strong force and the weak force behind some radioactive decay, reach no farther than a nucleus.

question: A helium nucleus is built of two protons and two neutrons. Measured with great care, it has a little less mass than two protons and two neutrons measured one by one, and the same shortfall turns up in every nucleus made of more than one particle. Physicists call it the mass defect. Why does a nucleus have less mass than its parts?
answer: Some of their mass left as energy when they joined
choices: Some of their mass left as energy when they joined
Some of their mass is stored inside it as heat
Packed tightly, the particles take up less room
Gravity pulls more weakly on particles packed tight
context: Albert Einstein's E = mc² says that mass and energy can turn into each other, and that a tiny mass is worth an enormous energy: one gram is worth about 90 trillion joules. When protons and neutrons bind into a nucleus, energy leaves and carries that sliver of mass away, so pulling the nucleus apart means putting the energy back; squeezing changes volume, not mass, and gravity changes weight, not mass. Chemical reactions shift mass too, but by about a billionth, far too little for any balance, which is why chemists find mass conserved.

question: Otto Frisch set out in Copenhagen in January 1939 to test the idea, his and Lise Meitner's, that a neutron can split a uranium nucleus in two. He lined a counting chamber with uranium, set a neutron source beside it, and made the counter record only pulses far bigger than uranium's own alpha particles could cause. Big pulses came. Which result would have counted most against the idea?
answer: Big pulses still coming with the neutron source taken away
choices: Big pulses still coming with the neutron source taken away
No big pulses at all once the uranium lining was taken out
Twice as many big pulses with paraffin wax round the source
Fewer big pulses whenever a weaker neutron source was used
context: No neutrons, no splitting: big pulses without the source would have meant something else was making them, but in hours of check runs Frisch saw none, and none without the uranium either. The count rose and fell with the strength of the source, and paraffin wax, which slows neutrons, doubled it, since slow neutrons split uranium more readily. Frisch called his pulses conclusive evidence that uranium nuclei were breaking into pieces of comparable size.

question: In a nuclear power plant, splitting uranium heats water into steam, and the steam spins a turbine that drives a generator. Operators set how fast the uranium splits by sliding control rods, made of materials such as boron or cadmium, in and out of the reactor's core. Dropped all the way in, the rods stop the chain reaction. How do they do it?
answer: They soak up neutrons before those split more nuclei
choices: They soak up neutrons before those split more nuclei
They slow the neutrons down so that fewer nuclei split
They cool the uranium until it stops splitting
They bounce the neutrons back out of the fuel
context: Boron and cadmium capture neutrons, and every neutron a rod soaks up is one that cannot split another uranium nucleus, so pushing the rods in slows the reaction and pulling them out speeds it up. Slowing neutrons is the moderator's job, usually the water round the fuel, and slow neutrons split uranium-235 more readily, not less; the same water carries the heat away to make the steam.

question: Fusion joins light nuclei into heavier ones. Fusion machines on Earth try to join deuterium and tritium, two heavy kinds of hydrogen, into helium, and they must first heat the fuel to 100 million degrees Celsius or more, until it is a plasma, a gas of bare nuclei and loose electrons. Why does fusion need such enormous heat?
answer: Only fast nuclei get close despite pushing each other away
choices: Only fast nuclei get close despite pushing each other away
Only very hot nuclei melt enough to flow into one another
Only great heat can break the nuclei into loose protons first
Only very hot fuel can burn with oxygen into helium
context: Every nucleus carries a positive charge, so two nuclei push each other away, and only nuclei moving very fast, which means very hot, come close enough for the short-range strong force to take hold. When deuterium and tritium fuse, the helium and spare neutron that come out have a little less mass than the fuel that went in, and the missing mass leaves as energy; nothing burns. Machines hold the hot plasma in strong magnetic fields, as in a tokamak, or crush tiny fuel pellets with lasers.

question: Scientists at the National Ignition Facility in California aimed 192 lasers at a tiny frozen pellet of deuterium and tritium, two heavy kinds of hydrogen, on 5 December 2022. The pellet's nuclei fused, and the team announced that for the first time a shot had reached ignition, a goal fusion scientists had chased for decades. What did ignition mean?
answer: The pellet gave out more energy than the lasers put in
choices: The pellet gave out more energy than the lasers put in
The laboratory made more energy than it drew from the grid
The fusion energy was sent out as electricity to homes
The pellet went on fusing by itself for hours afterwards
context: The fusion gave out 3.15 megajoules against the 2.05 megajoules of laser light fired into the tiny gold can that held the pellet, the first time any fusion experiment had got more energy out of its fuel than its lasers put in. But the lasers drew about 300 megajoules from the grid for that split-second shot, and no fusion machine yet makes more electricity than it uses, so whether fusion can power cities is still an open question. Later shots there have given out more than 8 megajoules.

question: Nuclear power plants make about a tenth of the world's electricity. A plant runs day and night whatever the weather, and over its whole life it gives off about as little carbon dioxide for each unit of electricity as a wind farm does. Every year or two, though, part of its fuel is used up and comes out of the reactor. What makes that used fuel hard to store?
answer: It stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years
choices: It stays dangerously radioactive for thousands of years
It is a liquid that can easily leak out of its tanks
It piles up by the millions of tonnes every year
It escapes from its casks whenever it is moved by road or rail
context: Used fuel is solid ceramic pellets sealed in metal rods; it cools for years in pools of water, which carry off its heat and block its radiation, and then goes into sealed casks of steel and concrete. All the used fuel American power plants have made since the 1950s would fit on one football field less than 10 yards deep, and thousands of cask shipments have crossed the country without any radioactive material escaping. It must be kept away from people for thousands of years: Finland has built the world's first deep underground store for it, but the United States still has no permanent store, its plan for one at Yucca Mountain halted since 2010.

question: A girl testing the lights for a model house joins three identical bulbs to a single battery, and all three light up. Then she tries unscrewing them one at a time. Whichever bulb she takes out, the other two stay lit. How must the three bulbs be wired?
answer: All three in parallel
choices: All three in parallel
All three in series
Two in series, the third in parallel with them
Two in parallel, the third in series with them
context: In parallel each bulb sits on a branch of its own with its own path to the battery, so taking one out leaves the other paths whole. In a single series loop any bulb taken out breaks the only path and all go dark, as on the old strings of holiday lights; with two in series, unscrewing one puts out its partner, and a bulb in series with the rest puts them all out.

question: A student lights a bulb with a battery and two wires. She has an ammeter, a meter that reads the current, the flow of charge, in amperes. She measures the current first in the wire leading into the bulb, then in the wire leading out of it, back to the battery. How do the two readings compare?
answer: The same, since no charge is used up in the bulb
choices: The same, since no charge is used up in the bulb
Lower leaving, since the bulb uses up some current
Lower leaving, since some charge becomes light
Higher leaving, since the bulb speeds the charge up
context: Every bit of charge that flows into the bulb flows out of it again, so the current is the same all the way round a single loop. What the bulb takes is energy, carried by the moving charge and given off as light and heat; the battery supplies energy, not a store of current that gets spent.

question: Two old bulbs with glowing filaments, one marked 60 watts and the other 25 watts, sit in two lamps plugged into sockets in the same house. The 60-watt bulb shines brighter, because more current flows through its filament. What does that extra current show about its filament?
answer: It has less resistance than the dim bulb's
choices: It has less resistance than the dim bulb's
It has more resistance than the dim bulb's
It gets more voltage than the dim bulb's
It holds more charge than the dim bulb's
context: Both bulbs get the same voltage from the house sockets, and with the same push more current flows only where there is less resistance: that is what resistance means. The brighter filament resists less, not more. A filament stores no charge; the charge flows through it, and what it gives off as light and heat is energy.

question: Georg Ohm, a teacher in Cologne, sent currents through wires of different lengths and thicknesses. His book of 1827 tied the current in a wire to the push driving it, now called the voltage, and to the wire's resistance. A reviewer in a Berlin journal called it "a web of naked fancies." Gustav Fechner put the rule to careful tests in 1831. Which result would have counted against Ohm?
answer: The same push, and more current, in a longer wire
choices: The same push, and more current, in a longer wire
The same push, and more current, in a shorter wire
The same push, and more current, in a thicker wire
Twice the push, and twice the current, in one wire
context: Ohm's law says the current rises in step with the push and falls as the resistance rises, and a wire of one metal resists more the longer it is and less the thicker it is, so at the same push a shorter or a thicker wire carries more current and a longer one less; only the longer wire with more current would break the rule. Fechner's measurements agreed with Ohm. The doubters' quarrel was mostly with treating electricity by mathematics, which most German physicists of the day did not do; the Royal Society gave Ohm its Copley Medal in 1841, and resistance is now measured in ohms.

question: Michael Faraday stood a magnet upright in a deep basin of mercury at the Royal Institution in September 1821, with its top just above the surface. He hung a wire from above so that its lower end dipped into the mercury, a liquid metal, beside the magnet. Then he sent a current from a battery down the wire. What did the wire do?
answer: It circled the magnet while the current ran
choices: It circled the magnet while the current ran
It swung onto the magnet and clung to it
It swung away from the magnet and hung there
It twitched once, then hung still beside it
context: A magnet pushes on a wire carrying a current at right angles to both the current and the magnet's field, so the wire is shoved sideways, never pulled in, and the mercury let it keep going round the pole without breaking the circuit. It was the first electromagnetic motor, the first steady motion made from a current and a magnet, and most motors since turn on the same sideways push, with coils in place of the wire.

question: Michael Faraday wound two separate coils of wire onto opposite sides of an iron ring on 29 August 1831. He connected one coil to a battery. The other had no battery of its own and ran to a galvanometer, a meter that detects current. When, if at all, did the galvanometer's needle move?
answer: Only as the battery was connected or disconnected
choices: Only as the battery was connected or disconnected
All the while the battery's current flowed
Never, since no wire joined the two coils
Only as the battery was connected, not disconnected
context: The needle flicked one way when the battery was connected and the other way when it was disconnected, and sat still while the current flowed steadily: the current in one coil made a current in the other only while it was changing, though no wire joined the two coils. Faraday's earlier tries with steady currents and magnets at rest had found nothing. Joseph Henry in Albany found the effect on his own, but his results came out in 1832, and the credit generally goes to Faraday.

question: Michael Faraday built a new machine in October 1831: a copper disc on an axle, between the poles of a horseshoe magnet. One sliding contact touches the axle and another the disc's rim, and wires from both run to a galvanometer, a meter that detects current. The disc is turned at one steady speed. What does the needle show while it turns?
answer: A current, for as long as the disc spins
choices: A current, for as long as the disc spins
One flick as it starts to turn, then nothing
Nothing, since the magnet itself never moves
A current only while the disc speeds up
context: As the disc turns, each part of the copper sweeps across the magnet's field, and a conductor moving through a magnetic field has a current driven along it, so the current flows for as long as the turning lasts. The magnet need not move: what counts is the motion of the copper through its field. It was the first electromagnetic generator, turning motion into electricity, though it gave only a small voltage.

question: On a long downhill road, the driver of an electric car lifts her foot off the accelerator. The car's electric motor, which had been driving the wheels, now holds the car back, so she hardly needs the brake pads. Nothing inside the motor has been rebuilt or swapped. What is the motor doing now?
answer: Working as a generator, charging the battery
choices: Working as a generator, charging the battery
Working as a motor, pushing back on battery power
Working as a brake, rubbing on its own shaft
Working as a magnet, gripping the steel axle
context: The turning wheels now spin the motor, so it makes a current that refills the battery, and the energy it takes from the car's motion slows the car: regenerative braking. One machine turns electricity into motion or motion into electricity, as Hippolyte Fontaine showed by accident at Vienna in 1873, when he wired an idle Gramme generator to a working one and its shaft began to spin. Friction brakes are still needed for a full stop, because the effect fades at low speed.

question: James Joule, a brewer in Salford, let weights fall to turn a paddle wheel in a can of water, and read the water's slight warming on a fine thermometer. He tried mercury too, and an iron wheel grinding on iron. Every way, close to 772 pounds falling one foot made enough heat to warm a pound of water by one degree Fahrenheit. What did that steady rate show?
answer: That work and heat are two forms of one thing
choices: That work and heat are two forms of one thing
That rubbing squeezes out heat stored in matter
That friction destroys a share of the work done
That falling weights make new energy as they fall
context: One exchange rate in water, in mercury and in rubbing iron meant the heat was not wrung from a store inside the matter but made from the work itself, with none of the work lost: energy changes form but is never made or destroyed, the first law of thermodynamics. Julius Robert Mayer, a German doctor who had sailed as a ship's doctor, had argued in 1842 that heat and work are one indestructible force, but it was Joule's measurements, set out in full in 1850, that persuaded physicists.

question: Count Rumford, who oversaw the boring of brass cannon at the arsenal in Munich, reported a test in 1798. A blunt borer was pressed hard into a cannon set in a box of cold water, and horses turned the cannon against it. Believers in caloric, a heat fluid, held that the grinding squeezed it out of the metal. Which finding did Rumford argue their idea could never explain?
answer: The heat kept coming for as long as the cannon turned
choices: The heat kept coming for as long as the cannon turned
The water came to the boil with no fire anywhere near it
The chips came off the brass hotter than boiling water
The water around the cannon kept all air from reaching it
context: A fluid squeezed out of the brass would have run out, but the heat seemed inexhaustible, and Rumford wrote that anything a body can go on giving without limit cannot possibly be a material substance; he could picture heat only as motion. Heat without fire, chips hotter than boiling water and the air shut out all fit a fluid squeezed from the metal, though he also found that the chips warmed water just as solid brass did, so nothing had been squeezed out of them. Believers in caloric held that their theory could be patched to fit, and it took James Joule's measurements in the 1840s to retire it.

question: Sadi Carnot, a French engineer, worked out in 1824 the most work a perfect engine, with no friction or leaks, can get from heat. Two such engines take in the same amount of heat. One works between steam at about 540 degrees Celsius and a cool river; the other between warm surface seawater and deep water about 20 degrees colder. Which gets more work from its heat?
answer: The steam engine, since its two sides differ more in temperature
choices: The steam engine, since its two sides differ more in temperature
The sea engine, since its heat is spread through far more water
Both the same, since both take in the same amount of heat
Both the same, since neither loses any work to friction
context: Carnot showed that the most work a perfect engine can get from heat is fixed solely by the temperatures of its hot and cold sides, whatever it runs on, and the wider the gap, the larger the share. On the sea's small gap even a perfect engine could turn only about 6 to 8 percent of its heat into work, while real coal plants turn about a third of theirs into electricity.

question: A fridge stands in a small, sealed room with well-insulated walls, its door propped wide open. Its motor runs without stopping, and cold air spills from the open door. After a few hours, how does the room's average temperature compare with when the fridge was switched on?
answer: Higher, since the work of pumping the heat ends up as heat too
choices: Higher, since the work of pumping the heat ends up as heat too
Lower, since the open fridge keeps sending its cold into the room
The same, since the fridge only moves heat and adds none
Lower, since the fridge destroys the heat it takes in
context: A fridge can move heat from cold to warm only by doing work, as Rudolf Clausius's statement of the second law requires, so it gives off more heat at its coils than it takes from inside. With the door open, the heat it pumps out flows straight back in, and the electrical energy its motor uses becomes heat as well, so the room slowly warms, though the air just in front of the door feels cool.

question: A car burns a tank of gasoline on a long drive and parks just where it started, no higher up and no faster than when it set out. What did the trip use up?
answer: None of the energy, but nearly all of its ability to do work
choices: None of the energy, but nearly all of its ability to do work
Most of the energy, destroyed as the fuel was burned
Most of the energy, destroyed by the rubbing of the brake pads
None of the energy, but all of the fuel's matter, burned to nothing
context: Energy is never destroyed, so all of it is still there, warming the air a little; but heat spread thinly through the air can do almost no work, and no engine can gather it up again to drive the car home. Physicists say the entropy has risen: the energy has become permanently unavailable to do work, which is what people really mean by losing or saving energy. Nor is the fuel's matter burned to nothing: its atoms leave the exhaust as carbon dioxide and water.

question: A film shows an egg rolling off a table and smashing on the floor. Run backwards, the film shows shell, yolk and white leaping up off the floor and closing into a whole egg on the table, something no one has ever seen happen. What keeps a broken egg from putting itself back together?
answer: Its pieces have far more ways to lie scattered than joined
choices: Its pieces have far more ways to lie scattered than joined
Putting it back together would take more energy than it has
The laws of motion work only forward, never in reverse
Gravity holds the pieces down and keeps them from rising
context: Each bump between two molecules obeys the laws of motion just as well run backwards, and the reversed film breaks no law of energy; what the egg obeys is the odds, since its pieces and the floor's warmth have vastly more ways to lie scattered than to come together, so entropy rises and the reverse is overwhelmingly unlikely rather than forbidden. Arthur Eddington called this one-way direction time's arrow in 1927, and why the universe began with entropy low enough for the arrow to start is still an open question.

question: Builders tried for centuries to make an overbalanced wheel turn forever. Its weights, on hinged arms, swing far out from the axle on the side going down and fold in close on the side coming up. Yet over a full turn the turning pulls of its two sides even out, and the wheel never runs on its own. What evens them out?
answer: The far-out side carries fewer of the weights
choices: The far-out side carries fewer of the weights
Gravity pulls more weakly on weights far from the axle
Friction at the axle holds back the far-out side
The axle sits off-centre, nearer the far-out side
context: A weight far from the axle turns a wheel harder, as on a seesaw, but the side where the arms swing out holds fewer weights than the side where they fold in, so the two turning pulls even out. Gravity pulls every weight alike, the wheel turns on its centre, and even on an axle with no friction at all it would gain nothing: over a full turn every weight is lifted as far as it falls. The Paris Academy of Sciences, refusing in 1775 to examine any more such machines, put it that an effect is always equal to its cause.

question: An inventor designs a ship that burns no fuel. Its engine draws in seawater, takes heat out of it, turns every bit of that heat into the work of driving the ship, and pours the chilled water out behind. Would such a ship break a law of thermodynamics?
answer: Yes, the second, though it would create no energy
choices: Yes, the second, though it would create no energy
Yes, the first, since it would create energy from nothing
Yes, the first, since it would destroy the heat it took in
No, since the heat in seawater is real energy it can use
context: The ship spends the sea's real heat, so it makes no energy from nothing and the first law has no quarrel with it; but no engine working round and round can take heat from one place and turn all of it into work, so this perpetual-motion machine of the second kind breaks the second law. Real ocean heat plants work only because they pump up cold water from the deep to serve as the colder side.

question: Students in a physics class take the turntable out of a microwave oven, lay a flat bar of chocolate inside and run the oven for a few seconds. Melted spots appear about 6 centimetres apart. Each gap is half a wavelength, so each wave is about 12 centimetres long. The label on the back gives the oven's frequency as 2,450 million waves a second. What do they find by multiplying those two numbers?
answer: The speed of the microwaves
choices: The speed of the microwaves
The energy of each microwave
The power of the oven
The time each wave takes to pass
context: Wave speed is frequency times wavelength: 2,450 million waves a second, each 0.12 metres long, make about 294 million metres a second, close to the 300 million metres a second at which light and every other electromagnetic wave crosses empty space. Real ovens heat unevenly, so the spots are not perfectly spaced and the result is only rough; measuring several gaps and averaging helps.

question: Thomas Young let a thin beam of sunlight in through a small hole in a window and held a slip of card, about a thirtieth of an inch wide, edgewise in it, as he described in 1803. In the card's shadow, where light passing its two sides overlapped, he saw bright and dark bands. When he blocked the light passing one side, the bands vanished. What was happening in each dark band?
answer: Light from the two sides met crest on trough and cancelled
choices: Light from the two sides met crest on trough and cancelled
Light from the two sides met and turned to heat there
Particles from the two sides collided and knocked each other away
The card's edges soaked up the light headed for those spots
context: Where light from one side arrives half a wave behind light from the other, crest meets trough and the two cancel, while light arriving in step adds into a bright band; nothing is turned to heat, for the energy missing from the dark bands shows up in the bright ones, and with one side blocked there is nothing left to cancel. Light added to light making darkness is what waves do, not a stream of particles, so the bands told against Isaac Newton's particle theory of light, though most scientists were won over only after Augustin Fresnel's and François Arago's work some fifteen years later. Light is now known to behave in some ways as a wave and in others as particles.

question: Noise-cancelling headphones carry a tiny microphone that hears the steady drone of a jet engine. A circuit turns the drone's wave upside down and plays it from the headphone's speaker, so each crest of the drone meets a trough and the drone almost vanishes. Suppose the circuit fell behind and its wave reached the ear exactly half a wave late. What would the listener hear?
answer: The drone, louder than with the speaker off
choices: The drone, louder than with the speaker off
The drone, cancelled just as well as before
The drone, cut to half its usual loudness
The drone, shifted up to a higher pitch
context: A wave turned upside down and then delayed by half a wave is back in step with the drone, so crest meets crest and the two add: constructive interference instead of destructive. The timing must be right, which is why such headphones do best on low, steady sounds like engine drone and worse on high or sudden ones, whose short or changing waves are harder to match. Paul Lueg patented the idea in 1936, and working versions followed in the 1950s.

question: Ian Donald, a Glasgow professor of midwifery, took fibroid tumours and an ovarian cyst removed from patients to a boilermaker's works at Renfrew in 1955. There a machine found hidden cracks in steel by the echoes of ultrasound pulses, and he tried it on the specimens, with a large steak for comparison. A cyst is a thin-walled sac of fluid. What echoes did the cyst give?
answer: Echoes from its near and far walls only
choices: Echoes from its near and far walls only
Echoes that faded steadily with depth
One strong echo from its near wall only
Echoes packed thickly from wall to wall
context: Fluid has no boundaries inside it, so the pulse sends back nothing until it reaches the cyst's far wall, leaving a clear gap on the screen; a solid tumour, in Donald's words, gave echoes that weakened steadily the deeper the sound went. Later his scanner showed that a woman thought to be dying of stomach cancer had a huge, harmless cyst instead, which surgeons removed. Donald, John MacVicar and Tom Brown published their scans in 1958, among them the first published ultrasound image of an unborn baby.

question: Robert Watson-Watt and Arnold Wilkins showed near Daventry, in England, on 26 February 1935 that a bomber about eight miles off sends back enough of a radio beam to be picked up. Within a year their test set was finding aircraft over 100 miles away. Yet ships hunting a submarine under the sea rely on the pulses of sound that sonar sends out. Why can radar not find the submarine there?
answer: Sea water soaks up radio waves within a short distance
choices: Sea water soaks up radio waves within a short distance
Steel hulls let radio waves pass straight through them
Sound travels through water faster than radio waves do
Radio waves need air to carry them along
context: Sea water carries electric current, so it drains a radio wave's energy within a short way, about a quarter of a metre for some radio waves and less still for radar's microwaves, while sound crosses kilometres of sea. Radio waves are far faster than sound, need no air at all and reflect strongly off metal, which is how radar finds ships and surfaced submarines. Watson-Watt had first been asked whether radio could be made into a death ray, and Wilkins worked out that it would take impossible amounts of power.

question: Charles Kao, an engineer at a laboratory in Harlow, England, argued in 1966 that a fibre of very pure glass could carry light for kilometres. Light sent into such a fibre runs along its central core of glass, striking the core's edge again and again. Why does the light not leak out of the core there?
answer: It meets the edge at too glancing an angle to cross
choices: It meets the edge at too glancing an angle to cross
A thin mirror coating round the core sends it back in
The core is too thin for light to slip out of it
Glass so pure lets no light out of the core
context: The core is wrapped in glass in which light travels a little faster, and light meeting that boundary at a glancing angle cannot cross it, so all of it is reflected back in: total internal reflection, with no mirror needed. Purity does a different job. Kao traced the fibres' heavy losses to traces of iron and water in the glass, which soaked up the light along the way and could be removed; Corning made a fibre purer than his target in 1970, and Kao shared the 2009 Nobel Prize in Physics.

question: Christoph Buys Ballot loaded trumpeters onto an open railway car in 1845 and had a locomotive pull them along the line between Utrecht and Maarssen while they held one steady note. Listeners beside the track heard the note about a half-tone higher as the train came toward them and a half-tone lower as it went away, as Christian Doppler had predicted three years before. Why did the note sound higher as the train came on?
answer: Each wave set out nearer, so the waves arrived bunched
choices: Each wave set out nearer, so the waves arrived bunched
The sound rode with the train, so it arrived faster
The note grew louder, and a louder note sounds higher
The rushing air pushed the trumpets' note higher
context: Each crest leaves the trumpet a little nearer the listener than the one before, so the crests arrive closer together, more of them each second, and the note is higher; behind the train they are stretched apart, and it is lower. The trumpets' own note never changed, and the sound's speed is set by the air, not by the train. Police radar guns and Doppler weather radar read the same shift in the echoes of microwaves and radio waves to tell how fast a car, or the rain in a storm, moves toward or away from them.

question: Repeaters stand along a long telephone cable, each one strengthening the fading signal before passing it on. An analog cable carries a call as a smooth wave shaped like the sound of the voice. A digital cable carries it as a code of on-and-off pulses, ones and zeros. Why does the digital call arrive clearer after many repeaters?
answer: Each repeater sends out fresh pulses, dropping the noise
choices: Each repeater sends out fresh pulses, dropping the noise
Each repeater boosts the pulses more than the noise
The pulses travel faster than the smooth wave does
The pulses pick up no noise at all along the cable
context: A pulse is either on or off, so a repeater only has to decide which, and noise too small to change that answer is dropped as it sends out a clean new pulse; an analog repeater amplifies the noise along with the voice, so the noise piles up stage after stage. Digital signals do pick up noise, but shrug it off up to that limit, and extra check bits catch many errors beyond it. Storing works the same way: each copy of a copy of a cassette tape grows hissier, while a digital recording can be copied again and again without loss.

question: Lithium, sodium and potassium are the first three alkali metals, going down their column of the periodic table. Dropped into water, lithium fizzes steadily, sodium reacts faster and hotter, and potassium reacts violently; caesium, further down the column, explodes. Why is each alkali metal more reactive than the one above it?
answer: Its outer electron is farther out and comes away more easily
choices: Its outer electron is farther out and comes away more easily
It has more outer electrons to give away to the water
Its nucleus has more protons, so it pulls the water apart
Its atoms are heavier, so they sink and meet more water
context: Every alkali metal has a single outer electron and reacts by giving it up. Each step down the column adds a shell, so that electron sits farther from the nucleus, screened from its pull by more inner electrons, and comes away more easily, though the nucleus holds more protons. Lithium, sodium and potassium are all less dense than water and float on it.

question: Fluorine, chlorine, bromine and iodine are the halogens, going down their column of the periodic table. Fluorine, at the top, is the most reactive of all the elements, and the halogens grow less reactive step by step down the column, the reverse of the alkali metals. Why is fluorine the most reactive halogen?
answer: Its small atom pulls hardest on an electron it takes in
choices: Its small atom pulls hardest on an electron it takes in
Its nucleus has the most protons, so it pulls hardest
It gives up its outer electrons more easily than the others
Its outer shell is nearer to full than the others' are
context: A halogen has seven outer electrons and reacts by taking in one more. Fluorine's outer shell lies closest to its nucleus, with the fewest inner electrons in the way, so it pulls a new electron in hardest; iodine has far more protons (53 against fluorine's 9), but its outer shell lies much farther out. All four halogens are one electron short of a full shell, and they react by taking electrons, not by giving them up.

question: From sodium to chlorine, across one row of the periodic table, each element has one more proton and one more electron than the one before, and the atoms grow heavier. Yet they shrink to about half the width. Why do they shrink?
answer: More protons pull harder on the same outer shell
choices: More protons pull harder on the same outer shell
More neutrons pull harder on the same outer shell
More electrons push the shells in toward the nucleus
More mass pulls the shells inward by its gravity
context: From sodium to chlorine every new electron goes into the same third shell while the inner shells stay as they are, so the growing positive charge of the nucleus draws that shell in: sodium's radius is about 190 picometres, chlorine's about 99. Neutrons carry no charge, electrons repel one another rather than push the shells inward, and gravity between such tiny masses is far too weak to matter.

question: Dmitri Mendeleev left an empty square below aluminium in his periodic table, and in 1871 he described the element that should fill it: an atomic weight of about 68, and about six times as dense as water. Paul-Émile Lecoq de Boisbaudran found gallium in 1875, and its atomic weight proved to be 69.7 and its density 5.9. Why did that forecast count as stronger evidence for the table than all the known elements it already fitted?
answer: It was made before the metal was found, so it could fail
choices: It was made before the metal was found, so it could fail
It proved that the table had no errors left anywhere in it
Its numbers fitted more closely than the known elements' did
It matched more properties than any known element had
context: A table built to fit the known elements was bound to fit them; a forecast set down before anyone had the metal could have been wrong, and it was not. The match was close, not exact, and Lecoq de Boisbaudran's first density, 4.7, was off: Mendeleev had written that the density would be 5.9, and when Lecoq de Boisbaudran measured again, on purer metal, he got 5.9. Gallium melts below 30 degrees Celsius, the low melting point he had forecast; scandium (1879) and germanium (1886) were still to come, not every forecast came true, and by 1890 the table was accepted as basic chemistry.

question: Henry Moseley fired electrons at one element after another in 1913 and measured the X-rays each gave off. The X-ray frequency climbed by one regular step from each element to the next. Cobalt weighs slightly more than nickel, yet its X-rays put it one step before nickel. What did that step show about cobalt?
answer: It has one proton fewer than nickel
choices: It has one proton fewer than nickel
It has one neutron fewer than nickel
It has one electron shell fewer than nickel
It has one outer electron more than nickel
context: Each step (strictly, in the square root of the frequency) is one more unit of positive charge in the nucleus, one more proton: cobalt has 27 and nickel 28, so the table is a count of protons, not an order of weights. Cobalt is the heavier because every cobalt atom carries 32 neutrons, while about two in three nickel atoms carry only 30, and the two share a row and so the same shells. Moseley did not measure tellurium and iodine themselves, and his paper kept tellurium first for its chemistry, but the same count, 52 protons against 53, puts it there.

question: Chemists of the early 1900s could not agree how many rare-earth metals ran from lanthanum to lutetium. The metals are so alike that chemists could not always tell a pure one from a mixture of two, and didymium, once taken for one element, proved to be two. Henry Moseley measured the X-rays they give off and showed that there must be exactly 15, counting both ends. How could X-rays settle what chemistry could not?
answer: Each element's X-rays rise one even step above the last's
choices: Each element's X-rays rise one even step above the last's
X-rays split a mixed sample into its separate rare earths
X-rays weigh each rare earth more exactly than any scales
X-rays count the neutrons in each rare earth's nucleus
context: Moseley's X-ray frequency rose by one even step per element, so every element took one whole number, with none skipped and none to spare: between lanthanum and lutetium there was room for exactly 15, however alike their chemistry. Number 61 was still empty, and his X-rays found it missing from Georges Urbain's samples; X-rays sort no samples, weigh nothing and follow the nuclear charge, not the neutrons. Moseley enlisted in the army in 1914 and was killed by a sniper at Gallipoli on 10 August 1915, aged 27.

question: Lord Rayleigh found that a litre of nitrogen taken from the air weighed about half a percent more than a litre made from chemicals. William Ramsay passed nitrogen from the air over heated magnesium, which combines with nitrogen, until only a little gas was left that would join with nothing he tried. In 1894 the two named it argon, from the Greek for lazy. What did argon turn out to be?
answer: The first of a family that the table lacked
choices: The first of a family that the table lacked
The element Mendeleev had left a gap for
A heavier form of nitrogen, not a new element
A new element in nitrogen's column of the table
context: Argon's weight, about 40, matched no empty square, and no column held anything so unreactive; Mendeleev at first argued it was a form of nitrogen. Ramsay found helium in 1895 and, with Morris Travers, neon, krypton and xenon in 1898, having forecast neon from the gap between helium and argon in Mendeleev's own way. Ramsay proposed a new column between the halogens and the alkali metals, and Mendeleev added it to his table in 1902.

question: A student looks through a prism at two lamps. The white-hot filament of an old light bulb spreads into a smooth band of every colour from red to violet. The thin glowing gas in a neon sign's tube breaks instead into many sharp bright lines, mostly red and orange. What do those lines show about neon's atoms?
answer: They give off energy only in set amounts
choices: They give off energy only in set amounts
They give off every colour, most too faint to see
They soak up most colours and give back the rest
They give off light only while the gas is burning
context: An electron in a neon atom can sit only at set energy levels, so when the current's electrons knock it up and it drops back, the atom gives off one set amount of energy, a photon of one exact colour; neon's set drops make its set lines, among them a bright red one at 640 nanometres. Between the lines the thin gas gives off no light at all, while the filament, a hot solid, glows in every colour at once. Nothing burns in the tube, and the light is the gas's own, not light it takes in from somewhere else.

question: An electron in a hydrogen atom, lifted to the third energy level, can fall straight back to the first and give off one ultraviolet photon. It can instead fall in two steps: to the second level, giving off a red photon, and then to the first, giving off another ultraviolet one. How do the two photons' energies together compare with the single photon's?
answer: The same, as both ways start and end at the same levels
choices: The same, as both ways start and end at the same levels
More, as two drops give off more energy than one
Less, as a red photon carries less energy than ultraviolet
Less, as some energy is lost in the stop between drops
context: A photon carries exactly the energy its electron loses in the fall, and the fall from the third level to the first is the same however it is made. In electronvolts, a tiny unit of energy, the red photon at 656 nanometres carries about 1.9 and the ultraviolet one at 121.6 carries 10.2, together 12.1, just what the single photon at 102.6 nanometres carries. Walther Ritz found such sums among the frequencies of spectral lines in 1908, five years before Niels Bohr's levels explained them.

question: A chemistry class dips clean wires into salts and holds each one in a Bunsen burner's flame. A strontium salt turns the flame crimson, a copper salt green-blue and a sodium salt bright yellow. Through a prism each colour breaks into thin lines, and no two metals' lines fall in the same places. Why does each element give off colours of its own?
answer: Its electrons' energy levels are spaced in its own way
choices: Its electrons' energy levels are spaced in its own way
It burns in the flame at a temperature of its own
It strains its own colours out of the flame's light
Its atoms' weight sets the colours that they give off
context: An electron can only drop between its own atom's levels, and each element's levels are spaced differently, so its drops, and the colours they give, are its alone: sodium's two yellow lines sit at 589.0 and 589.6 nanometres. The flame's heat only lifts the electrons and does not choose the colour, and firework makers rely on the same fact, with strontium for red, copper for blue and sodium for yellow. Lithium also turns a flame crimson, so a careful chemist checks the lines as well as the colour.

question: Joseph von Fraunhofer, a Bavarian lens maker, found hundreds of dark lines in sunlight in 1814. Later he fixed a prism to a telescope and turned it on the night sky. The light of the Moon, Venus and Mars showed the Sun's own dark lines, while the bright stars Sirius and Castor showed lines unlike the Sun's. Where must those lines of Sirius and Castor have been made?
answer: In the stars, before their light set out
choices: In the stars, before their light set out
In Earth's air, as their light came down
In the prism, as their light passed through
In the lens, as their light was gathered
context: The Moon and the planets shine by sunlight they reflect, so they carry the Sun's lines; the stars' light came through the same air, prism and lens, so lines found in Sirius and Castor but not in sunlight had to be made in the stars. Fraunhofer had already got the same lines in sunlight with different glass, which ruled out flaws in it, though two broad bands at the red end of sunlight really are made by oxygen in Earth's air. He never learned what made the lines, and died in 1826.

question: Auguste Comte wrote in 1835 that the chemical make-up of the stars could never be studied by any means. A flame coloured with sodium shows two bright yellow lines in exactly the place of the two dark D lines in sunlight. Gustav Kirchhoff sent bright sunlight through such a flame into his spectroscope in 1859, and the dark D lines grew darker. What did that show?
answer: Sodium gas soaks up the very colours it gives off
choices: Sodium gas soaks up the very colours it gives off
The flame's glare makes the lines look darker by contrast
The flame's heat bends the yellow sunlight off its path
Sunlight's yellow waves cancel out the flame's yellow
context: A gas takes up light of exactly the energies its electrons can jump by, the same energies it gives off when they drop back, so a sodium flame with brighter light behind it cuts dark lines where its bright ones would be. The Sun's glowing surface shines out through cooler gas above it, and Kirchhoff concluded that sodium is in the Sun's atmosphere. Comte had died in 1857, two years before the Sun's chemistry was first read from its light.

question: Pierre Janssen in India in August 1868, and Norman Lockyer in England that October, saw a bright yellow line in the light from the Sun's edge. It lay close to sodium's two yellow lines but on neither, and Lockyer named the element he believed made it helium, after the Greek word for the Sun. The idea met doubt, and even mockery, for 27 years. What finally settled the question?
answer: A gas from a uranium mineral glowed with that line
choices: A gas from a uranium mineral glowed with that line
The line turned up in the light of other stars too
The line was seen again at every eclipse that followed
A gas from a natural gas well glowed with that line
context: William Ramsay treated cleveite, a uranium mineral, with acid in March 1895 and collected a gas whose glow showed the Sun's yellow line, and Lockyer and William Crookes confirmed it as helium; helium was found in natural gas, its main source today, only in 1905, in wells drilled in Kansas. A line seen again at eclipses or in other stars showed only that the line was real, not what made it. The doubters had reason to wait: a green line in the Sun's corona was blamed on a new element, coronium, until it turned out in the 1930s to be iron stripped of 13 electrons by the corona's heat.

question: Hydrogen's dark lines are strong in the spectrum of Sirius, weaker in the Sun's and weaker still in Betelgeuse's. Cecilia Payne, at Harvard in 1925, read such lines with Meghnad Saha's new theory of how atoms lose electrons. What did she find mostly sets how strong the lines are?
answer: How hot the star's surface is
choices: How hot the star's surface is
How much hydrogen the star holds
How big the star is
How old the star is
context: Astronomers had long taken a strong line to mean a lot of an element. In the hottest stars nearly all the hydrogen has lost its electron and can make no lines, and in cooler stars such as the Sun nearly all of it sits in its lowest level, where it cannot take up visible light; only near 10,000 kelvins, about the heat of Sirius's surface, are many hydrogen atoms ready to make the lines. Read this way, stars turned out to differ mainly in temperature and to be made mostly of hydrogen and helium, and about 73 percent of the Sun's mass is now known to be hydrogen.

question: The Space Shuttle rode into orbit on three main engines that burned liquid hydrogen with liquid oxygen, and the two gases joined to make water. A student writes the reaction as H2 + O2 → H2O, then counts two oxygen atoms on the left of the arrow and only one on the right. Which equation balances it?
choices: H2 + O2 → H2O2
H2 + O2 → 2H2O
context: Only the numbers in front may change: 2H2 + O2 → 2H2O has four hydrogen atoms and two oxygen atoms on each side, so no atom, and no mass, is made or lost. Writing H2O2 also evens the count, but it turns the product from water into hydrogen peroxide, a different substance.

question: Hydrochloric acid is a strong acid, and sodium hydroxide is a strong base. A chemist adds the base to the acid in a flask, a few drops at a time, until exactly enough has gone in to neutralise it. What does the flask hold at the end?
answer: A salt and water
choices: A salt and water
A salt and hydrogen gas
Water and hydrogen gas
The same acid and base, only watered down
context: Neutralising makes new substances: the acid's hydrogen ions join the base's hydroxide ions as water, and the sodium and chloride that remain are sodium chloride, table salt, dissolved in it. Chemists call every such product a salt, and each acid and base gives its own. No gas comes off, and once exactly enough base has gone in, neither the acid nor the base is left, only salt water.

question: A student sets up three test tubes, each with an iron nail, and leaves them for several days. In the first, the nail lies in water that was boiled to drive out its air, under a layer of oil. In the second, it sits in dry air over calcium chloride, which soaks up water. In the third, it lies in plain water open to the air. Only the third nail rusts. What does the first tube rule out?
answer: That water without oxygen can rust iron
choices: That water without oxygen can rust iron
That oxygen without water can rust iron
That water and oxygen together rust iron
That iron needs salt in the water to rust
context: Boiling drives the dissolved air out of the water and the oil keeps air from dissolving again, so the first nail has water but no oxygen, and it stays bright. The dry tube is the one that rules out oxygen alone, and the third shows that the two together are enough; salt is not needed, though salt water makes iron rust faster still.

question: Chemists find that warming many reactions by 10 degrees Celsius, from 20 degrees to 30, roughly doubles how fast they go. Yet in a gas at 30 degrees the particles collide less than 2 percent more often than at 20. What explains most of the faster rate?
answer: Many more of the collisions are energetic enough to react
choices: Many more of the collisions are energetic enough to react
The energy a collision needs in order to react becomes smaller
The particles swell up and make larger targets to strike
The particles break up into smaller pieces that move faster
context: A reaction happens only when particles collide with at least a minimum energy, the activation energy. Warming barely changes how often they meet but greatly raises the number of fast, energetic particles, so many more collisions clear that bar, which itself stays where it was; only a catalyst offers a lower one. The particles themselves do not swell or break up.

question: Gus Grissom, Ed White and Roger Chaffee died in a fire inside their Apollo 1 spacecraft during a launch-pad test in January 1967. The cabin was filled with pure oxygen, a little above the pressure of the air outside, and once what was most likely an electrical spark set nylon and foam alight, flames filled it within half a minute. Air is only about one-fifth oxygen. Why does fuel burn so much faster in pure oxygen?
answer: More oxygen molecules strike the fuel every second
choices: More oxygen molecules strike the fuel every second
Oxygen itself burns, as a second fuel beside it
Oxygen molecules move faster than nitrogen ones
Oxygen acts as a catalyst that speeds the burning
context: Burning happens where oxygen molecules meet the fuel, and pure oxygen crowds about five times as many into each litre as air does, so collisions with the fuel come far more often and the fire races. Oxygen does not burn, and it is used up feeding the fire, so it is no catalyst; at the same temperature its molecules are, if anything, a little slower than nitrogen's. NASA afterwards launched its crews in a mix of 60 percent oxygen and 40 percent nitrogen.

question: Fine sawdust lying in a heap on a workshop floor only smoulders when a spark lands on it. Blown up into a cloud, the same sawdust can burn so fast that it explodes, and flour mills and grain elevators face the same danger from their dust. Why does the cloud burn so much faster than the heap?
answer: The flying specks each meet the air all round
choices: The flying specks each meet the air all round
The flying specks rub together and grow hot
The flying specks move fast, so they burn hotter
The flying specks break into finer dust as they fly
context: Burning happens only where the fuel's surface meets oxygen: in a heap the air reaches only the specks on top, while in a cloud every speck is wrapped in air, so the whole surface of every speck burns at once and the flame races through. The specks are the same wood; what changes is how much of their surface the air can reach. A spark lit the flour dust hanging in the Washburn A Mill in Minneapolis on 2 May 1878, and the blast and fire killed 18 people; most deaths in such disasters come from a second blast, when the first shakes settled dust up into the air.

question: Hydrogen peroxide breaks down into water and oxygen on its own, but so slowly that little changes in a bottle on the shelf. A pinch of black manganese dioxide powder makes it froth with oxygen within seconds. A student wants to know whether the powder is a catalyst or one more reactant. Which result would show that it is a reactant?
answer: Less powder is left once the frothing stops
choices: Less powder is left once the frothing stops
The frothing stops once the peroxide runs out
More powder makes the peroxide froth faster
The flask grows warm while the peroxide froths
context: A reactant is used up as it turns into products; a catalyst is not. Filtered out, washed and dried, the manganese dioxide weighs just what it did before and sets fresh peroxide frothing again, so it is a catalyst, while the frothing's end, its speed and its warmth would fit either one. Catalase, an enzyme in blood and liver, speeds the same breakdown in living things, and the platinum, palladium and rhodium of a car's catalytic converter clean exhaust gas the same way, without being used up.

question: A plant turns much of the glucose its leaves make into starch, long chains of glucose packed into grains, and stores it in its roots, seeds and tubers. Why does the plant keep its store as starch rather than as the glucose itself?
answer: Packed in grains, it draws no extra water into the cells
choices: Packed in grains, it draws no extra water into the cells
Packed in grains, it also builds the walls of the cells
Packed in grains, it gives energy without being broken down
Packed in grains, it travels easily to the rest of the plant
context: Glucose dissolved in a cell's water would add to what is dissolved inside, and water would flow in by osmosis until the cell swelled; starch does not dissolve, so a plant can pack a great deal of it away without upsetting its water balance. The plant breaks starch back into glucose when it needs the energy, and its sugar travels as sucrose, not starch. Its cell walls are cellulose, another chain of glucose, whose links let the chains lie straight and bind into strong fibres.

question: The human body keeps some of its reserve energy as glycogen in the liver and muscles, and most of it as fat, in its fat cells. Why is the bulk of the reserve kept as fat?
answer: Gram for gram, it packs in far more energy
choices: Gram for gram, it packs in far more energy
Gram for gram, it gives up its energy faster
Gram for gram, it turns into glucose more easily
Gram for gram, it holds more water for the cells
context: A gram of fat holds more than twice the energy of a gram of glycogen, and fat is stored dry, while each gram of glycogen is held with three or four grams of water. Glycogen is the quick store: a branched chain of glucose, broken down fast when the body suddenly needs it, and the liver's supply lasts only half a day to a day, while most of a fat molecule can never be turned into glucose at all.

question: Evert Gorter and François Grendel took red blood cells from people and several other mammals in 1925. A mammal's mature red blood cell has no nucleus and no inner membranes. The two men dissolved the fat out of the cells, spread it on water as a film one molecule thick and found that it covered about twice the cells' total surface. What did they conclude about the cell membrane?
answer: It is a double layer of fat molecules
choices: It is a double layer of fat molecules
It is a single layer of fat molecules
It is fat on one face and protein on the other
It holds only half the cell's fat, the rest lying inside
context: With no inner membranes, all of a red blood cell's fat lies in its outer membrane, so a film that covers twice the cells' surface means the fat around each cell is stacked two molecules deep. Each phospholipid's water-loving head faces the watery fluid on one side or the other, and its two oily tails turn inward. Their solvent missed about a quarter of the fat and their measurements made the cells look smaller than they are, but the two errors roughly cancelled, and the double layer has stood.

question: Proteins do much of the work in living things, as enzymes, in the muscle that contracts, as the keratin of hair and as antibodies. Frederick Sanger spent from 1943 to 1955 on insulin, a small protein from cattle. He broke its chains into short pieces in several ways and worked out what each piece was made of. What did his finished result show about a protein?
answer: It is a chain of amino acids in one exact order
choices: It is a chain of amino acids in one exact order
It is a mix of chains that vary from molecule to molecule
It is a chain of amino acids repeating one short pattern
It is a chain of sugars with amino acids hung along it
context: Fitting the overlapping pieces together, Sanger found insulin to be two chains, of 21 and 30 amino acids, each in a fixed order, and by extension every kind of protein has its own exact sequence; many chemists had thought proteins somewhat shapeless, mixtures that varied from molecule to molecule. A chain folds into a shape set by that order, and the shape fits the protein for its job. Sanger won a Nobel Prize for the work in 1958.

question: Friedrich Miescher found deoxyribonucleic acid (DNA) in white blood cells in the 1860s, and Phoebus Levene later showed that it is a chain built from four kinds of nucleotide. A protein is a chain too, built from about 20 kinds of amino acid. Into the 1940s, most biologists expected genes to be made of protein. Why did protein seem the likelier material?
answer: More kinds of unit could make far more different chains
choices: More kinds of unit could make far more different chains
More kinds of unit could store more energy in each chain
More kinds of unit could make each chain harder to break
More kinds of unit could let each chain copy itself
context: Genes must carry a vast store of varied instructions, and twenty kinds of unit seemed to promise far more variety than four; Levene even took DNA for a plain repeat of its four nucleotides, chemically far too simple to carry genes. Experiments in 1944 and 1952 showed that genes are DNA after all, and Erwin Chargaff found that its four nucleotides are not present in equal amounts. Strung in any order along a very long chain, four kinds of unit can spell out endless different messages, and ribonucleic acid (RNA) carries copies of them to where proteins are built.

question: A cell in the human body holds about 30 times as much potassium as the fluid around it. Potassium leaks slowly out through its membrane all the time by diffusion, from more crowded to less, yet the difference lasts. Which observation would show that the cell keeps the difference up by active transport?
answer: A poison that cuts off its energy supply lets the difference fade
choices: A poison that cuts off its energy supply lets the difference fade
A tear made in its membrane lets the difference fade
Warming the cell makes the potassium leak out faster
More potassium in the fluid outside slows the leak
context: Active transport spends the cell's energy to carry a substance against the crowd, from less to more, so cutting off the energy lets the leak win and the difference runs down; poisons such as cyanide stop it in just this way. A tear, warmth or extra potassium outside each changes the leak, which is diffusion and needs no energy. The pump that carries potassium in and sodium out was found by Jens Christian Skou in crab nerves in 1957, and it uses a large share of the energy many cells spend.

question: Salt sprinkled on a garden slug makes it pour out slime, and it dies within minutes. Salt on a person's hand does no such harm. What makes the difference?
answer: Its skin lets water pass out very easily
choices: Its skin lets water pass out very easily
Its slime reacts with the salt to form a poison
Its skin soaks up the salt, which poisons its cells
Its skin lets the salt in, and water floods in after it
context: Salt dissolves in the slug's slime, making a brine saltier than the inside of its body, and water flows out of its skin cells toward the salt by osmosis until it shrivels and dies of drying out; Gordon Port of Newcastle University says the salt simply draws the water out of the slug's skin. A person's skin lets far less water through. Red blood cells in strong salt water shrink the same way, and in pure water they swell and can burst.

question: Martinus Beijerinck found in 1898 that the sap of tobacco plants with mosaic disease, which mottles the leaves, still made plants sick after it passed through a filter that holds back bacteria. Then he infected a healthy plant with the filtered sap, used sap from that plant to infect another, and so on down a line of plants. The disease did not fade down the line. Why did that rule out a poison as the cause?
answer: A poison would have been watered down at every step
choices: A poison would have been watered down at every step
A poison could never have passed through the filter
A poison would have killed the plants, not mottled them
A poison would have stayed in the first plant it reached
context: Each plant received only a little of the sap of the one before, so a fixed dose of poison would have thinned out until the disease faded; instead the agent was multiplying inside each living plant. Dissolved poisons do pass such filters, as diphtheria toxin does, which is why the filter alone could not decide. Beijerinck found the agent would grow in no broth, only in living, growing tissue, and he named it a virus.

question: Wendell Stanley purified the cause of tobacco mosaic disease in 1935 into fine, needle-shaped crystals, like those of a pure chemical. Dissolved and applied to healthy leaves, the crystals still gave them the disease. Most biologists do not count a virus such as this one as a living thing. What is their main reason?
answer: It can copy itself only inside a living cell
choices: It can copy itself only inside a living cell
It is far too small to count as a living thing
It is pure protein, with no genes inside
It never changes from one generation to the next
context: A virus is genetic material, DNA or RNA, in a coat of protein, with no ribosomes or energy-making chemistry of its own: outside a cell it does nothing, and inside one it makes copies with the cell's own machinery. Size is not the test, for some giant viruses are bigger than the smallest bacteria, which are alive; Stanley first took his crystals for pure protein, but they were soon found to hold RNA, and viruses do evolve, often fast. Whether they are alive is still argued, and some biologists place them at the very edge of life.

question: A boy has a runny nose and a sore throat from a cold, and his mother asks the doctor for an antibiotic. Penicillin, one of the best known, kills bacteria by wrecking the wall that each one builds around itself as it grows. The doctor says no antibiotic can cure a cold. What is the reason?
answer: A virus has none of the parts such drugs attack
choices: A virus has none of the parts such drugs attack
A virus has grown resistant to all such drugs
A virus is too small for such drugs to hit
A virus multiplies too fast for such drugs
context: Antibiotics strike parts that bacteria have and human cells lack, such as the wall penicillin wrecks and the bacteria's own ribosomes. A cold virus has no wall and no ribosomes; it copies itself with the machinery of the boy's own cells, so the drug has nothing to hit. An antibiotic taken for a cold does no good and adds to the overuse that breeds resistant bacteria.

question: Alexander Fleming found a blue-green mould growing on a dish of staphylococcus bacteria in his London laboratory in September 1928, and the bacteria around it had been destroyed. What he saw could not show whether the killing needed the living mould itself. Which test could answer that?
answer: Test the broth it grew in, with the mould filtered out
choices: Test the broth it grew in, with the mould filtered out
Repeat the same dish many times, each with fresh mould
Grow the mould and the bacteria together for longer
Set the mould on a dish of a different kind of bacteria
context: Fleming did just that: the clear, straw-coloured 'mould juice' that came through the filter still worked against staphylococci, streptococci and pneumococci, so the killer was a substance the mould gives off, not the living mould. Repeating the dish, letting it grow longer or setting the mould on other bacteria all leave the living mould and the killing together, so none can tell them apart. In March 1929 he named the substance penicillin, in place of the clumsy phrase 'mould broth filtrate'.

question: Alexander Fleming named his mould's bacteria-killing substance penicillin in a paper of 1929. Yet for about ten years after that, almost no one used it to treat a sick person. What held it back?
answer: No one could purify it before it broke down
choices: No one could purify it before it broke down
It harmed white blood cells as well as germs
A patent kept other laboratories from making it
It sickened the animals it was injected into
context: Penicillin falls apart quickly, and neither Fleming's assistants nor Harold Raistrick's team in 1932 could get it out of the mould broth pure. It did not harm white blood cells, nor the mice and rabbits Fleming injected, and no patent stood in the way: Fleming sent samples of his mould to other researchers, and patents on ways of making penicillin came only in the 1940s, in the United States. From 1939 Ernst Chain, Howard Florey and Norman Heatley at Oxford found how to extract and keep it, the work that the press long credited to Fleming alone.

question: Howard Florey's team at Oxford, among them Ernst Chain and Norman Heatley, gave eight mice a deadly dose of streptococcus bacteria on 25 May 1940, then gave four of them penicillin. By the early hours of the next morning, all four untreated mice were dead and the four treated ones were alive. What did this show that Alexander Fleming's own tests had not?
answer: That it could save an animal from an infection
choices: That it could save an animal from an infection
That it did an animal no harm when injected
That it worked against streptococci, not only staphylococci
That it would cure sick people as it cured mice
context: Fleming had shown that penicillin worked against streptococci as well as staphylococci in a dish and did injected mice and rabbits no harm, but he never treated an infected animal, the crucial step; the four untreated mice proved the dose of bacteria was deadly. Whether it would cure people too had still to be tried, and the first patients were treated early in 1941. The 1945 Nobel Prize went to Fleming, Florey and Chain, and the rule of three winners at most left Heatley out.

question: Doctors at a hospital find a gene for resisting one antibiotic in two kinds of bacteria that are not close relatives, and its DNA is the same in both, base for base. Within a few years the gene has spread through both kinds. How did it most likely come to be in both?
answer: Bacteria passed copies of it directly to one another
choices: Bacteria passed copies of it directly to one another
Each kind evolved it on its own under the drug
The antibiotic changed both kinds' genes the same way
Both kinds inherited it from a shared ancestor
context: Bacteria can hand genes to other living bacteria, even of another kind, often on plasmids, small extra loops of DNA passed from cell to cell; this sideways sharing is the main way resistance spreads, and the same gene, base for base, in distant kinds is its mark. A gene handed down from so distant an ancestor would no longer match, new resistance mutations are too rare (at most about one cell in a million each generation) to build the same gene twice, and an antibiotic writes no genes: it only favours cells that already carry one. Animals, as a rule, pass genes only down to their young; bacteria also pass them sideways.

question: Vanessa D'Costa and her colleagues studied genetic material (DNA) from ground in the far north that had stayed frozen for 30,000 years, long before anyone made an antibiotic drug. Mammoth DNA in it, and none from moose or spruce, showed the DNA was ancient, not modern. Among the old genes were ones that let bacteria resist modern antibiotics, vancomycin among them. Why did bacteria carry such genes so long ago?
answer: Soil microbes have long made antibiotics against one another
choices: Soil microbes have long made antibiotics against one another
Chance mutations made them, with no antibiotics to favour them
The ice-age cold changed their genes to make them hardier
Bacteria make genes in advance for dangers still to come
context: Most antibiotics are natural weapons: soil microbes such as Streptomyces make them to hold back rival microbes, so genes that resist them were favoured in the soil 30,000 years before the first antibiotic drug. Neither a drug nor the cold writes new genes, and bacteria cannot plan ahead; a drug kills the cells that lack resistance and leaves those that carry it to multiply. The find is no reason to relax, for heavy use in hospitals and on farms favours these old defences all the more.

question: Walther Flemming, who named mitosis in 1882 after the threads he saw in stained salamander cells, called interphase, the long stretch between two divisions, a resting stage. Alma Howard and Stephen Pelc later gave the root tips of broad beans radioactive phosphorus, which a cell builds into new DNA, and tracked which nuclei took it up. When did the root cells copy their DNA?
answer: During part of interphase, before mitosis begins
choices: During part of interphase, before mitosis begins
During prophase, as the threads first thicken
During anaphase, as the threads are pulled apart
At a steady rate, all through the cycle
context: The label went into the nuclei during one part of interphase, Flemming's resting stage, before any threads appeared. Howard and Pelc named that part the S phase, for synthesis, with gaps called G1 and G2 before and after it. Interphase fills about nine tenths of a cell's cycle as it grows and copies its DNA, so every chromosome is already double when mitosis begins.

question: Partway through mitosis, a cell's chromosomes line up across its middle. Each chromosome is now two identical halves, and spindle fibres reaching from opposite ends of the cell take hold of one half each. The cell waits in this stage, metaphase, until every chromosome is held from both ends, and a single loose one can keep it waiting. What does the wait guard against?
answer: A new cell getting both copies of a chromosome
choices: A new cell getting both copies of a chromosome
A new cell being too small when it splits off
Two chromosomes trading pieces of their DNA
A break in the DNA being passed on
context: Each chromosome was copied in interphase, and in anaphase its two copies are pulled to opposite ends of the cell, so only when every chromosome is held from both ends does each new cell get one copy of each. Moving on too soon can leave one new cell with an extra chromosome and the other one short, an error common in tumour cells. A cell's size and any broken DNA are weighed at other checks, before the DNA is copied or before mitosis begins, and trading pieces belongs to meiosis, not mitosis; in telophase a nucleus forms round each set.

question: At the end of its division, an animal cell is pinched in two as a ring of protein fibres tightens round its waist like a drawstring. A cell in the growing tip of an onion root is enclosed in a cell wall. Once its nucleus has divided, how does that cell split in two?
answer: It builds a new wall from the centre outward
choices: It builds a new wall from the centre outward
It grows a new wall inward from its old one
It pinches in, drawing its wall in with it
It buds off a small new cell through its wall
context: Small sacs from the Golgi apparatus gather in the middle of the cell and fuse into a cell plate, which spreads outward until it meets the old wall and becomes a new wall between the two daughter cells. The wall is too stiff to be pinched in, and the water pressure inside a plant cell pushes back as well, so the new wall starts at the centre, not at the old wall. This last step, cytokinesis, leaves two cells with identical nuclei.

question: Many chemotherapy drugs, given to fight cancer, also harm healthy parts of the body. Patients often lose their hair while taking them, and their bone marrow makes fewer new blood cells. Why are the hair roots and the marrow hit?
answer: Their cells divide again and again
choices: Their cells divide again and again
Their cells soak up and store the drug
Their cells take in the most blood
Their cells no longer obey signals to stop
context: Such drugs work by stopping cells from dividing, so they strike the healthy tissues that make new cells all the time as well as the cancer: the hair roots, the lining of the gut, renewed every few days, and the marrow, which must replace red blood cells that last only about four months. Mitosis gives the body the cells it needs to grow, mend wounds and replace worn ones, though most nerve cells and heart muscle cells never divide again once they mature. Ignoring the signals to stop is the mark of cancer cells, not of healthy marrow.

question: John Gurdon aimed ultraviolet light at a frog's egg to destroy its nucleus, then put in its place the nucleus of a gut cell from a feeding tadpole; a few such eggs grew into swimming tadpoles. The gut cells came from tadpoles with a mutation that leaves one nucleolus in each nucleus, where normal frogs have two; the eggs came from normal frogs. The new tadpoles' cells had one. Critics doubted his 1962 result. Which doubt did the single nucleolus settle?
answer: That the egg's own nucleus had built the tadpole
choices: That the egg's own nucleus had built the tadpole
That a stray unspecialised cell gave the nucleus
That only a rare few gut nuclei could do it
That the light had harmed the rest of the egg
context: Tadpoles carrying the donor's mark had been built by the gut cell's nucleus, not by any part of the egg's own that had lived through the light. The mark could not show that the gut cell had been fully specialised, for a stray unspecialised cell from the same tadpole would carry it too, so a team in Basel later did the experiment with the nucleus of a white blood cell making antibodies, and again got tadpoles. Gurdon shared the 2012 Nobel Prize with Shinya Yamanaka for showing that mature cells can be reprogrammed.

question: Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi put 24 genes, all busy in embryonic stem cells, into fibroblasts, cells of connective tissue, taken from mice. A very few of the cells were reset into stem cells able to become any kind of cell in the body. In the same study, published in 2006, they ran the test again and again, each time leaving out one gene, and narrowed the 24 to four that were each needed. Which test would show that those four were enough?
answer: Put in the four alone, with none of the other 20
choices: Put in the four alone, with none of the other 20
Put in each of the four on its own, one at a time
Leave out all four at once, keeping the other 20
Put in all 24 again, into many more cells
context: Only the four put in with none of the others can show that they are enough, and they were: Oct3/4, Sox2, Klf4 and c-Myc together reset a few cells. Leaving genes out shows only which are needed, and the team had found that no gene put in on its own reset a single cell. The reset cells are called induced pluripotent stem cells; one of the four, c-Myc, can drive cancer, so later recipes leave it out at the cost of a slower, rarer reset.

question: Leland Hartwell and Ted Weinert hit baker's yeast with X-rays, which break DNA. Normal cells halted before dividing, and the more harm was done, the longer they halted. Cells with a broken RAD9 gene did not halt; they kept dividing for a few generations and died. Yet when the two held X-rayed cells of that kind for several hours with a drug that blocks division, the cells mended their DNA. What is the RAD9 gene's job?
answer: Making the cell wait until the damage is mended
choices: Making the cell wait until the damage is mended
Mending the breaks that X-rays make in the DNA
