Shielding the cell's DNA from the X-rays
Pushing the cell on to its next division
context: Held still, the cells without a working RAD9 could mend their DNA, so the gene does not do the mending: it holds the cell back until the mending is done, and without that wait the cells divided with broken DNA and died. Hartwell called such controls checkpoints, and he shared the 2001 Nobel Prize with Paul Nurse, who found the enzyme that drives a cell through its cycle, and Tim Hunt, who found cyclins, proteins that build up through each cycle and are destroyed at every division. A human cell whose checkpoints fail can go on dividing with damaged DNA, one of the steps toward cancer.

question: Normal cells taken from an animal's tissue and grown in a dish of food spread and divide until they cover the bottom in a single layer, each touching its neighbours. There they stop, though food remains. Cells taken from a cancer are grown in the same way. What do they usually do?
answer: Go on dividing, and pile up over one another
choices: Go on dividing, and pile up over one another
Go on dividing, but die as fast as they form
Stop at a single layer, but reach it sooner
Stop at a single layer of much larger cells
context: Normal cells stop dividing once they are crowded, but cancer cells usually lose this check and grow over one another, which is what a cancer is: cell division that no longer stops when it should. Cancer cells often divide quickly, and they can ignore the signals that tell a cell to die, but what marks them out is that they do not stop when there are enough of them. In the body the same failure piles extra cells into a tumour, a crowd of cells, not a layer of swollen ones.

question: Oswald Avery's team reported in 1944 that purified DNA passed an inherited trait between strains of bacteria, yet many biologists suspected protein in the samples. Alfred Hershey and Martha Chase tested it in 1952 with a virus that infects bacteria: DNA in a protein coat. They tagged the DNA of some viruses with radioactive phosphorus and the coats of others with radioactive sulfur, let them infect bacteria, then shook off the empty coats. Which finding would have pointed to protein as the genetic material?
answer: Sulfur inside the bacteria, and phosphorus outside
choices: Sulfur inside the bacteria, and phosphorus outside
Phosphorus inside the bacteria, and sulfur outside
Both tags inside the bacteria, in equal shares
Both tags outside, along with all the empty coats
context: Sulfur marks the protein and phosphorus the DNA, so the genetic material is whichever tag goes into the cells and is passed on to the new viruses. Hershey and Chase found the reverse of the protein result: about four-fifths of the phosphorus stayed with the bacteria, and some of it turned up in the new viruses, while most of the sulfur stayed outside with the coats. That helped settle the doubt Avery's critics had raised: genes are made of DNA.

question: Erwin Chargaff, at Columbia University, measured the four bases of DNA around 1950: adenine (A), thymine (T), guanine (G) and cytosine (C). Human DNA came out about 31 percent A, 29 percent T, 20 percent G and 20 percent C. DNA from the bacterium E. coli came out about 25 percent A, 24 percent T, 26 percent G and 26 percent C. Which pairing across DNA's two strands explains both sets of figures?
answer: A with T, and G with C
choices: A with T, and G with C
A with G, and T with C
A with C, and G with T
A with A, and G with G
context: Only A with T and G with C fits both: in human DNA, A and T match at about 30 percent and G and C at about 20, while in E. coli all four sit near a quarter, so that species alone could not tell the pairings apart. Each A on one strand faces a T on the other, and each G a C, so the amounts of A and T must match, and of G and C, in every species, even though the share of A and T differs from one species to the next. Watson and Crick built this pairing into their double helix in 1953 and cited Chargaff's matching ratios.

question: Rosalind Franklin and her student Raymond Gosling made an X-ray photograph of DNA at King's College London in May 1952, later known as Photo 51. Its cross of dark spots marked a helix. Maurice Wilkins also worked on DNA at King's. James Watson, who was working out DNA's structure with Francis Crick at Cambridge, saw the photograph on a visit to King's in January 1953. How did he come to see it?
answer: Wilkins showed it to him without telling her
choices: Wilkins showed it to him without telling her
Gosling showed it to him, with her leave
Franklin showed it to him and explained it
He took a print from her desk while she was away
context: As Franklin prepared to leave King's, Gosling passed the photograph to Wilkins, who showed it to Watson without telling her: nothing was taken from her desk, but she was not asked, and Crick also saw her measurements in a report that Max Perutz passed him. Watson and Crick's paper thanked Wilkins, Franklin and their co-workers only for a knowledge of 'the general nature' of their unpublished results, while Franklin and Gosling's own paper ran in the same issue. Franklin died in 1958, aged 37, four years before Watson, Crick and Wilkins shared a Nobel Prize.

question: Watson and Crick's 1953 paper noted that their base pairing 'immediately suggests a possible copying mechanism for the genetic material.' Matthew Meselson and Franklin Stahl tested copying at the California Institute of Technology. They grew bacteria on heavy nitrogen, so their DNA was heavy, then moved them to ordinary nitrogen for one round of copying and sorted the DNA by density in a spinning tube. Suppose each old double helix stayed whole and each copy was built all new. What would the tube have shown?
answer: Two bands, heavy and light, in equal amounts
choices: Two bands, heavy and light, in equal amounts
Two bands, heavy and light, with far more light
One band, halfway between heavy and light
Two bands, halfway and light, in equal amounts
context: Under that idea each old heavy helix would sit beside one new light one, so the tube would hold heavy and light bands in equal amounts, with light pulling ahead only in later rounds. Meselson and Stahl found a single band halfway between, so the idea was wrong; after a second round, half the DNA was halfway and half light, just as expected if the two strands part and each is given a new partner built by base pairing. Each old strand serves as the template that the 1953 sentence hinted at.

question: A cell copies a gene into messenger RNA (mRNA), the working copy that carries the gene's instructions to the ribosomes. The RNA is built along one strand of the gene's DNA, each new base pairing with the DNA base it faces, except that RNA uses uracil (U) where DNA uses thymine (T). One stretch of that DNA strand reads T-A-C-G-G-A. What does the messenger RNA built along it read?
answer: A-U-G-C-C-U
choices: A-U-G-C-C-U
A-T-G-C-C-T
U-A-C-G-G-A
T-A-C-G-G-A
context: Each base of the messenger pairs with the DNA base it faces: A with T, G with C, C with G, and U, standing in for T, with A, so T-A-C-G-G-A gives A-U-G-C-C-U. Copying the strand letter for letter, or only swapping its T for U, makes a strand that matches it instead of pairing with it. A-U-G is the start signal at which a ribosome begins to build a protein.

question: Francis Crick, Sydney Brenner and two colleagues worked in 1961 with proflavin, a chemical that adds or removes a single base in DNA, on a gene of a virus that infects bacteria. One extra base in the gene wrecked the protein it made, and so did two. Three extra bases gave a working protein again, with one extra amino acid. What did this show about how a cell reads a gene?
answer: In words of three bases, from a fixed start
choices: In words of three bases, from a fixed start
In words of two bases, each overlapping the next
In words of three bases, each overlapping the next
One base at a time, each base its own word
context: Each added base shifts how every base after it is grouped into words, so one or two extras garble the rest of the gene; a third puts the grouping back in step after it, so the gene works again. That works only if the words are three bases long, do not overlap and are counted from a fixed starting point. Four kinds of base in words of two would make only 16 words, too few for 20 amino acids, while words of three make 64.

question: Vernon Ingram, at Cambridge, compared haemoglobin, the protein that carries oxygen in red blood cells, from healthy people and from people with sickle-cell disease in 1956. He cut each with an enzyme into short pieces and sorted the pieces into a pattern of spots. The two patterns matched in every spot but one. What did that one piece of the sickle-cell protein hold?
answer: One amino acid in place of another
choices: One amino acid in place of another
One amino acid missing from the chain
One extra amino acid added to the chain
The same amino acids in a new order
context: Ingram and his colleagues found that valine stood where glutamic acid should be, at the sixth place in each of haemoglobin's beta chains of 146 amino acids: the gene's word G-A-G had become G-T-G, one base swapped for another. Valine shuns water, so when the haemoglobin gives up its oxygen it sticks to its neighbours, and the molecules stack into long fibres that bend the cell into a stiff sickle. Ingram was the first to show that one changed amino acid in a protein can cause a disease.

question: Alec Jeffreys, at the University of Leicester, saw on an X-ray film in September 1984 that DNA could be sorted into a pattern that differs from person to person, a DNA fingerprint. To make one, DNA is cut into pieces and set in a slab of gel, and an electric current pulls the pieces through it toward the positive end, since DNA carries a negative charge. A long piece carries more charge than a short one, yet the short pieces travel farthest. Why?
answer: The gel's mesh holds long pieces back more
choices: The gel's mesh holds long pieces back more
Short pieces carry more charge for their length
Short pieces weigh less, so the pull moves them faster
The gel's own charge holds long pieces back more
context: Charge and size grow together, so in plain liquid long and short pieces of DNA move at about the same speed; the gel, a tangle of fibres that works like a sieve, slows the long pieces more by its mesh, not by any charge of its own, and the pieces spread out by size. Jeffreys's pieces came from repeated stretches of DNA whose lengths differ from person to person, so the bands fall in a different pattern for each person. In 1985 such a pattern showed that a boy whose family came from Ghana was closely related to his family in Britain.

question: August Weismann, a German biologist, argued in the late 1800s that the cells which become eggs and sperm must pass through a 'reduction division' that halves their number of chromosomes. Each human body cell holds 46 chromosomes, and at fertilisation an egg and a sperm join into one cell. Why must the sex cells carry only half?
answer: To keep the count from doubling every generation
choices: To keep the count from doubling every generation
To give the child an equal share from each parent
To weed out harmful genes before they pass on
To let the child keep the stronger copy of each gene
context: If eggs and sperm kept all 46 chromosomes, a child's first cell would hold 92, and the count would double again in every generation; meiosis halves it to 23 in each sex cell, so the child starts with 46 again. Each parent would give an equal share with or without the halving, and the halving does not pick out the healthy copy of a gene or the dominant one. Edouard Van Beneden had already seen, in the eggs of a roundworm in 1883, two divisions that halve the number.

question: Thomas Hunt Morgan and his students at Columbia University bred fruit flies by the thousand in milk bottles. The fly's genes for white eyes and for miniature wings both lie on its X chromosome, and in 1911 Morgan found that the two traits passed down together more often than chance would give. Yet some young flies got one trait without the other. How did Morgan explain those flies?
answer: The paired chromosomes had swapped matching pieces
choices: The paired chromosomes had swapped matching pieces
A new mutation had changed one of the two genes
One of the two genes had moved to another chromosome
Stray flies from other bottles had got mixed in
context: Morgan proposed crossing over: in meiosis the two partners of a pair lie side by side, break and trade matching stretches, so a gene for white eyes can end up on one chromosome with a gene for normal wings. Frans Janssens had described the X-shaped crossings, chiasmata, in 1909, and in 1931 Harriet Creighton and Barbara McClintock saw the swapped pieces under the microscope in maize. A mutation changes a gene, while crossing over only regroups genes already there, so the chromosomes passed on can be new patchworks of the two partners.

question: Alfred Sturtevant, a student in Morgan's laboratory, put his homework aside one night in 1911 to draw the first map of genes on a chromosome. He took how often crossing over split two genes on the fly's X chromosome as a measure of how far apart they lie. Testing three genes at a time, he found that the percentage for one pair came out close to the sum of the percentages for the other two pairs. What did that show?
answer: The genes lie in a line, each in a fixed place
choices: The genes lie in a line, each in a fixed place
The genes lie in a clump, with no fixed order
The genes shift place from one fly to the next
The genes are spaced evenly along the chromosome
context: Only along a line does the distance between two genes equal the sum of their distances to a third gene lying between them; in a clump, or with genes that moved, the percentages would not add up, and adding fixes an order, not equal gaps. Genes far apart are split more often because more of the places where the partners may swap lie between them. His 1913 map placed five genes of the X in an order later confirmed, and one percent of crossing over is now called a centimorgan.

question: Gregor Mendel crossed a pea plant with round yellow seeds and one with wrinkled green seeds, and every seed of the first generation came out round and yellow; round and yellow are the dominant traits. He let those plants pollinate themselves and sorted 556 of the seeds they bore. About what share were round and green, a mix that neither of the first two plants had?
answer: About three in sixteen
choices: About three in sixteen
About one in sixteen
About one in four
About nine in sixteen
context: About three seeds in four are round and, on its own, about one in four is green, so about 3/4 x 1/4 = 3/16 are round and green; Mendel counted 108 of the 556. His full count, 315 round yellow, 108 round green, 101 wrinkled yellow and 32 wrinkled green, is close to 9:3:3:1, so nine in sixteen is the round yellow share, and the new mixes show that the genes for shape and colour sort into sex cells independently. Had the two traits travelled as a pair there would have been none, and genes lying close together on one chromosome come near that, giving only a few.

question: A snapdragon that breeds true for red flowers, crossed with one that breeds true for white flowers, gives offspring with pink flowers. Neither allele of the colour gene masks the other, so a plant with one of each comes out in between. A grower crosses two of the pink plants and raises their seeds. How should the flowers of the new plants come out?
answer: About one red to two pink to one white
choices: About one red to two pink to one white
All of them pink, like both of their parents
About three pink to one white
Half red and half white, with no pink
context: Each pink parent passes on its red allele or its white allele by chance, so about one seedling in four gets two reds, two in four get one of each and come out pink, and one in four gets two whites. Red and white come back because the alleles never blended; only their effect in a plant with one of each is in between, a pattern called incomplete dominance. Carl Correns found the same pattern in the four o'clock flower in the early 1900s.

question: Karl Landsteiner, working in Vienna, mixed the serum, the liquid part of the blood, of himself and his colleagues with one another's red cells in 1900 and 1901. Some mixes clumped, and he sorted people into groups A, B and C, later renamed O. His students Alfred von Decastello and Adriano Sturli then tested 155 people and found four whose red cells were clumped by group A serum and by group B serum alike. What did those red cells carry?
answer: Both the A marker and the B marker
choices: Both the A marker and the B marker
Neither the A marker nor the B marker
One marker halfway between A and B
A third marker, unlike both A and B
context: Group A serum attacks the B marker and group B serum attacks the A marker, so cells clumped by both carry both, and the group was named AB; it is group O cells that carry neither and are clumped by neither serum. An AB person carries an A allele and a B allele, and each makes its own marker in full, a pattern called codominance, unlike the pink snapdragon's in-between colour. By showing which donors suit which patients, Landsteiner ended the lottery of transfusion, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1930.

question: Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil von Dungern showed in 1910 that the A, B and O blood groups are inherited, and they then proposed two genes, each carried in two copies: one for A or no A, and one for B or no B. Felix Bernstein, a German mathematician, argued in 1924 for a single gene with three alleles, A, B and O, of which each person carries two. Which finding in families could tell the two ideas apart?
answer: Whether an AB parent ever has a group O child
choices: Whether an AB parent ever has a group O child
Whether two group O parents ever have a group A child
Whether two group A parents ever have a group O child
Whether an A parent and a B parent have an AB child
context: Under the two-gene idea an AB parent who carries a no-A copy and a no-B copy can pass on both together, so an O child is possible; Bernstein's AB parent has only an A allele and a B allele to give, so every child gets one or the other. The other three findings fit both ideas equally well. Counts of the groups in whole populations, and the families studied after, bore Bernstein out, apart from very rare exceptions found much later, and the ABO gene is now known to lie on chromosome 9.

question: Queen Victoria never showed signs of haemophilia, an inherited illness in which the blood fails to clot properly, and no case is known in her family before her. Yet her son Leopold had it, and two of her daughters, Alice and Beatrice, who never showed it either, had sons who did. What best explains that pattern?
answer: Victoria carried the faulty gene on one of her X chromosomes
choices: Victoria carried the faulty gene on one of her X chromosomes
Victoria carried the faulty gene on both of her X chromosomes
Her husband, Prince Albert, carried the faulty gene and passed it on
The faulty gene arose new in Leopold, by chance
context: A carrier passes her faulty X to about half her children: a son who gets it has the illness, and a daughter who gets it becomes a carrier in turn, as Alice and Beatrice did. Two faulty copies would have made Victoria ill herself; a father gives his sons his Y, so Albert could not have given it to Leopold; and a change arising new in Leopold could not reach his sisters' sons. Through her daughters it reached the royal families of Russia and Spain; a genetic study of the Romanov remains in 2009 showed it was haemophilia B, and it most likely began as a new mutation in Victoria or her father, though no one can be sure.

question: Charles Darwin worked out natural selection in 1838 and kept it unpublished for twenty years. Then, in June 1858, a letter from Alfred Russel Wallace, posted from Ternate in the Malay islands, brought him the same idea, reached on its own. Their papers were read together at the Linnean Society of London on 1 July. Each man had found his key in an essay by Thomas Malthus. What did Malthus argue?
answer: People multiply faster than their food supply
choices: People multiply faster than their food supply
Earth is shaped by slow change over vast ages
Organs grow with use, and the gain is handed on
Every creature is designed to fit its way of life
context: Malthus argued in 1798 that population tends to grow faster than its food, so that famine, disease and war must hold it back. Darwin, reading him in September 1838, saw that in such a struggle favourable variations would tend to be preserved and unfavourable ones destroyed, and Wallace thought of Malthus's checks on population while ill with fever in February 1858. The slow change of Earth came from Charles Lyell, use and inheritance from Jean-Baptiste Lamarck, and design from William Paley.

question: Suppose biologists follow one herd of wild sheep on an island for thirty years, catching, weighing and taking blood from every animal they can. They record four changes over that time. In the sense biologists give the word, which of the changes is evolution?
answer: A gene for dark wool grows more common in each crop of lambs
choices: A gene for dark wool grows more common in each crop of lambs
Each adult's genes for thick wool switch on as winters turn colder
The herd doubles in size after a run of mild winters
Lambs grow heavier in wet years and lighter in dry ones
context: Biologists define evolution as a change, over generations, in a population's genes: how common each version of a gene is. A herd can double, its lambs can fatten in wet years and every sheep's body can answer the cold, all without changing which genes the next generation carries, so none of those is evolution. Selection acts on single animals, but only a population evolves, as the share of each gene version shifts from one generation to the next.

question: Suppose a river changes course and cuts a population of field mice in two. The halves never meet again for thousands of generations, and each changes in its own way. Then biologists bring mice from the two sides together. Which finding would show that the halves have become separate species?
answer: Their hybrid young cannot have young of their own
choices: Their hybrid young cannot have young of their own
Their hybrid young look like neither of their parents
Their fur now differs in its colour and in its length
They now feed mostly on quite different kinds of seeds
context: Biologists count two populations as one species while they can interbreed and have fertile young, so the test is whether genes can still pass between them: horses and donkeys mate, but their young, mules, are sterile, so they are two species. Species are not defined by looks, so fur, food and the look of the hybrid young can all differ while populations stay one species, and look-alike populations can be separate species. Separated populations that change until they can no longer interbreed have become new species; that is speciation.

question: Hunters killed northern elephant seals for the oil in their blubber until, by the 1890s, perhaps as few as twenty were left. Protected from the 1920s, the seals now number over 200,000, yet one stretch of their DNA comes in just two types, where 48 southern elephant seals showed 26. Either the hunting left them so alike, or the species always was. Which evidence could settle it?
answer: DNA from seals that died before numbers crashed
choices: DNA from seals that died before numbers crashed
DNA from many more of the seals that are alive today
DNA from many more southern elephant seals
DNA from the seals first protected in the 1920s
context: Only seals that lived before the crash can show what the species once carried, and DNA from museum skins and old bones holds more variety than seals today: the few survivors carried only some of the gene versions, and the rest were lost by chance. That is genetic drift, change by chance, which is strongest in small populations, and a crash like this is called a bottleneck. Seals of the 1920s and today descend from the few survivors, and more southern seals could not settle it either, since two species can differ for other reasons.

question: A typhoon swept over Pingelap, a small atoll in the Pacific, in 1775, and only about twenty people lived through it. Today as many as one islander in ten is totally colour-blind, unable to see any colour at all, while in the United States the condition strikes about one person in 33,000. What best explains why it is so common on the island?
answer: One of the few survivors happened to carry its gene
choices: One of the few survivors happened to carry its gene
The storm and famine spared those who carried its gene
Glare from the sea and sand damaged islanders' eyes
The hardship after the storm made its gene arise anew
context: The ruler of the day, one of the survivors, is believed to have carried one copy of the gene, which does no harm alone; among so few people chance let it spread until about three islanders in ten carry it, and marriages among relatives brought pairs of copies together. That is genetic drift after a bottleneck, the founder effect: in a small population chance can make even a harmful gene common, and people with the condition see poorly in bright sunlight. The condition is inherited, not caused by glare, and it came down from that survivor, not from new mutations after the storm.

question: Scientists published the chimpanzee's genome in 2005 and lined it up against the human one. Letter for letter, about 98.8 percent of the DNA that lines up is the same; counting the stretches one species has gained or lost, the figure is nearer 96 percent. Human and mouse DNA differ about sixty times as much. What does this pattern show?
answer: Humans and chimpanzees had a recent common ancestor
choices: Humans and chimpanzees had a recent common ancestor
Humans descend from chimpanzees like those of today
Chimpanzees are slowly evolving to become humans
Humans and chimpanzees grew alike by living alike
context: Small changes build up in DNA generation by generation, so two lines that split long ago differ more: the human and chimpanzee lines parted about six to seven million years ago, the mouse line about 75 million. Both lines have changed since their split, so chimpanzees are cousins, not ancestors, and neither is turning into the other. Living alike does not make two genomes match letter for letter; the 98.8 and 96 percent figures are two ways of counting the same comparison.

question: In one of Richard Lenski's twelve flasks of Escherichia coli (E. coli), cells that could feed on citrate appeared around generation 31,500. Citrate had been in the broth since 1988, but E. coli normally cannot use it where there is oxygen. Zachary Blount thawed frozen samples from that flask's past and regrew them in many cultures. Citrate eaters arose again only from samples taken at generation 20,000 or later. What did that show?
answer: An earlier genetic change had paved the way
choices: An earlier genetic change had paved the way
One rare mutation could have come at any time
Long years among citrate taught the cells to use it
The oldest samples had been harmed by the freezing
context: Trillions of cells from the first 15,000 generations never found the trick, so it was not one rare mutation equally likely at any moment: some change by generation 20,000 had prepared the way, and the population's history mattered. The final step was itself a mutation, a duplicated stretch of DNA that put a citrate-carrying gene beside a switch that works in oxygen. Bacteria do not learn a new food, and frozen samples stay alive: a fossil record that can be brought back to life.

question: August Weismann cut the tails off white mice and bred them, then cut the tails off their young in turn, for five generations. Stories told of a tailless cat whose kittens had no tails. Yet all 901 of Weismann's young mice were born with tails of full length. Which idea of heredity did his result support?
answer: Egg and sperm carry traits, set apart from the body
choices: Egg and sperm carry traits, set apart from the body
Every part of the body sends particles to egg and sperm
A parent's body hands on the changes it goes through
A child's traits are an even blend of its parents'
context: Weismann argued that heredity runs through the germ plasm of egg and sperm, kept apart from the body, so a wound to the body never reaches it; the result counted against Lamarck's inheritance of acquired traits and Darwin's own gemmules, and said nothing either way about blending. Lamarck's idea was a respectable rival, held in part even by Darwin, and critics fairly noted that a cut tail is an injury, not a change built by use. What retired it was genetics, which found traits passed in genes through egg and sperm; a few chemical marks on DNA can pass on for a generation or two, but they do not revive Lamarck's theory.

question: Antoine Lavoisier suspected that breathing is a slow burning of carbon. With Pierre-Simon Laplace, in the winter of 1782 to 1783, he shut a guinea pig for ten hours in a chamber packed round with ice and weighed the water from the ice its body heat melted; in separate trials they measured the fixed air, now called carbon dioxide, that it breathed out. They burned charcoal in such a chamber too. Which result would back Lavoisier's idea?
answer: As much ice for each ounce of fixed air as burning charcoal melts
choices: As much ice for each ounce of fixed air as burning charcoal melts
Far less ice for each ounce of fixed air, as breathing is so slow
As much ice for each hour as a lump of burning charcoal melts
Far less ice for each hour than a lump of burning charcoal melts
context: The guinea pig melted about 13 ounces of ice in ten hours, and charcoal giving off as much fixed air melts about 10, as close a match as Lavoisier could hope for, so he wrote that respiration is a combustion, very slow but like the burning of carbon. Burning the same amount of carbon gives the same heat whether it goes slowly or fast, so the fair test is per ounce of fixed air; the ice melted in an hour depends only on the size of the lump and how fast each one gives off heat, so more or less of it says nothing about whether the animal burns carbon. Aristotle and Galen had taught that breathing cools the blood; the slow burning is now known to run, step by step, in the mitochondria of the body's cells.

question: In cellular respiration, glucose and oxygen become carbon dioxide and water, and the energy released is stored in a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). A runner breathes in oxygen with every stride and breathes out carbon dioxide. In the reactions of respiration, where do the atoms of the oxygen she breathes in end up?
answer: In the water made in the mitochondria
choices: In the water made in the mitochondria
In the carbon dioxide she breathes out
In the ATP made in the mitochondria
In the glucose stored in her cells
context: At the end of the chain of reactions on the inner membrane of the mitochondria, each oxygen molecule takes up electrons and hydrogen ions and becomes water; it is the only step in breaking down glucose that uses the oxygen breathed in. The carbon dioxide breathed out is built from the glucose's own carbon, split off in the mitochondria, and no oxygen gas goes into ATP or glucose. Respiration runs roughly as photosynthesis in reverse, which splits water and gives its oxygen off as gas.

question: Louis Pasteur grew yeast in sugar solutions around 1860. Spread thin in a shallow dish open to the air, the yeast grew faster and fermented less; shut away from air in a sealed flask, it fermented hard and used far more sugar for each gram of yeast it grew. A cell stores the energy it frees from sugar in a molecule called adenosine triphosphate (ATP). Why does yeast without oxygen need so much more sugar to grow?
answer: Each sugar yields far less ATP without oxygen
choices: Each sugar yields far less ATP without oxygen
Each ATP it makes does less work without oxygen
Its enzymes are used up faster without oxygen
It splits sugar to free the oxygen it lacks
context: Fermenting a molecule of glucose yields only 2 ATP, while respiring it fully with oxygen in the mitochondria yields many times more, about 30 in human cells and up to about 18 in yeast, so a yeast cell without air must break down far more sugar for the same energy and the same growth. Each ATP holds the same energy however it was made, enzymes are not used up, and fermentation frees no oxygen: it keeps the first steps of breaking down sugar running and gives off alcohol and carbon dioxide. Biologists call oxygen's brake on fermentation the Pasteur effect.

question: A girl runs her first long race, and two days later her legs ache more than ever. Until the 1980s, many blamed such aches on lactic acid, or lactate, which muscle cells make by fermentation when they run short of oxygen. Why do most exercise scientists now reject that idea?
answer: It is back to normal within an hour, long before the ache peaks
choices: It is back to normal within an hour, long before the ache peaks
It stays in the leg muscles for days, yet it causes no pain there
Trained runners make none of it, yet they get the ache too
Its level in the blood never rises, even in a hard race
context: Blood lactate rises in hard running, in trained runners as in beginners, and falls back to normal within about an hour, while the ache builds over the first day and is worst one to three days later; and exercise in which muscles shorten makes lactic acid too without leaving them sore. The ache is thought to come instead from tiny tears in the muscle fibres, mostly in work where muscles lengthen as they pull, such as running downhill, and from the inflammation that follows: in a 1983 test, an easier downhill run left legs sore and a harder level run did not. Lactic acid does form in hard-working leg muscles, and the liver turns much of it back into fuel.

question: Eduard Buchner ground yeast with quartz sand and squeezed out its juice under great pressure in 1897. Mixed with cane sugar, the juice gave off carbon dioxide for days, as living yeast does. Buchner said that a substance dissolved in the juice did the work, while followers of Louis Pasteur held that fermentation needs the living yeast cell. Which result would have counted most against Buchner?
answer: Filtered of all its yeast cells, the juice did not ferment
choices: Filtered of all its yeast cells, the juice did not ferment
Boiled for a few minutes first, the juice did not ferment
Kept on ice for two weeks, the juice still fermented well
Given milk sugar in place of cane sugar, the juice did not ferment
context: A few living cells slipping through the press would have explained everything, so juice passed through a filter that holds back every yeast cell was the deciding test; Buchner's filtered juice still fermented, and he named the dissolved agent zymase, a protein, winning the 1907 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. Boiling, cold and a sugar the juice could not use fit either idea, since heat wrecks a protein as surely as it kills a cell. Zymase proved to be a team of enzymes that, in living yeast, does its work inside the cell.

question: Emil Fischer reported in 1894 on two forms of methyl glucoside, a compound of glucose. The two hold the very same atoms, arranged a little differently. An enzyme from yeast split one form and left the other untouched, while emulsin, an enzyme from almonds, split only the other. By Fischer's account, why could each enzyme split only one form?
answer: Only that form fitted the enzyme's own shape
choices: Only that form fitted the enzyme's own shape
Only that form held its atoms loosely enough
Only that form dissolved readily enough in water
Only that form gave out energy as it was split
context: Fischer wrote that an enzyme and the molecule it works on must fit together like a lock and its key. The two forms differ only in which way one group points from the ring, yet that was enough to shut one enzyme out and let the other in; had looseness, dissolving or energy decided it, both enzymes would have split the same form. Daniel Koshland refined the picture in 1958 with induced fit: the enzyme's working pocket, its active site, is not rigid but closes snugly around the right molecule as it binds. That fit is why each enzyme is said to be specific to its own substrate.

question: A jar of dry glucose can sit on a laboratory shelf without changing, though glucose gives out a great deal of energy when it burns. Inside a cell at 37 degrees Celsius, enzymes break glucose down in a chain of quick steps. How does an enzyme speed up its step?
answer: It lowers the energy needed to start the step
choices: It lowers the energy needed to start the step
It supplies the energy needed to start the step
It raises the energy that the step gives out
It warms the molecules taking part in the step
context: Every reaction, even one that gives out energy, needs a push to start, its activation energy; an enzyme offers an easier path with a far smaller push, so the step runs millions of times faster at body heat, and the enzyme itself comes out unchanged. It gives no energy of its own and leaves the energy the step gives out just as it was. Heating a cell enough to drive such reactions without enzymes would wreck its parts.

question: A man with the flu runs a fever of 39 degrees Celsius, a rise set by his brain that is thought to help him fight the virus. A body held at about 42 degrees or more, from heat stroke or an extreme fever, is in grave danger of brain damage and death. What goes wrong inside its cells at such a heat?
answer: Their enzymes lose the shape their work depends on
choices: Their enzymes lose the shape their work depends on
Their enzymes are used up faster than new ones are made
Their DNA splits apart into its two strands
Their outer membranes stiffen and let nothing pass
context: Heat shakes the folded chain of an enzyme loose, so its active site loses the shape that fits the molecules it works on; above about 40 degrees proteins begin to unfold, and held at 42 or more, cells and organs fail. A wrong pH bends enzymes out of shape in the same way, which is why each works best in its own range. The two strands of DNA stay joined until far hotter than 42 degrees, heat makes membranes looser, not stiffer, and heat does not use enzymes up; a fever is a rise the brain sets on purpose, while heat stroke is the body's heat control failing.

question: A coal fire gives off its heat as its fuel joins with oxygen from the air. Lord Kelvin, one of the leading physicists of the 1800s, showed in 1862 that the Sun cannot be shining by any burning of that kind. What was his reason?
answer: It would have burned out in a few thousand years
choices: It would have burned out in a few thousand years
It holds none of the oxygen that any burning needs
No fire could stay lit in the cold of empty space
Its ash would long since have smothered its fire
context: Kelvin worked out that even the most powerful chemical burning would give only about 3,000 years of the Sun's heat, far too short for Earth's long history. The Sun does hold oxygen, the third most common element in it after hydrogen and helium, and a fire with oxygen of its own burns in empty space, as a rocket engine's does. Kelvin turned instead to the Sun's slow shrinking, which still gave it only some tens of millions of years.

question: Ray Davis caught neutrinos, tiny particles that stream out of the Sun's core, in a tank of chlorine-rich fluid deep in a gold mine. He counted only a third as many as models of the Sun predicted. Neutrinos come in three kinds, and chlorine catches only one. Canada's Sudbury Neutrino Observatory found in 2001 and 2002 that all three kinds together match the models' total, though only a third are of Davis's kind. Which explanation of his shortfall did that leave standing?
answer: They change kind on their way from the core
choices: They change kind on their way from the core
The Sun's core makes fewer than the models said
Most of them decay away on their way to Earth
Davis's tank had miscounted the one kind it caught
context: The Sudbury Neutrino Observatory, 2,100 metres down a nickel mine in Ontario, watched 1,000 tonnes of heavy water. Its first results in 2001, set beside the count of the Super-Kamiokande detector in Japan, and its own count of all three kinds in 2002 showed the models' full number arriving, but only about a third as electron neutrinos, the one kind chlorine catches: the rest had changed kind on the way, which means neutrinos have mass. Most physicists had suspected Davis's count or the models of the core, and both were cleared; Davis won a share of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Physics, and SNO's Arthur McDonald a share of the 2015 prize.

question: Light from the Sun's surface crosses to Earth in about eight minutes. The energy it carries was made in the core long before: by most estimates its trip out took from about ten thousand to well over a hundred thousand years, most of that time in the dense layers around the core. Why is the trip out so slow?
answer: The light is soaked up and sent off again in random directions
choices: The light is soaked up and sent off again in random directions
Hot atoms jostle their neighbours, passing it on by conduction
The Sun's strong gravity keeps pulling the light back down
It waits in the core until enough builds up to break out
context: The gas around the core is so dense that light goes only a tiny way before an atom soaks it up and sends it off again in a new direction, so the energy zigzags outward like a lost walker; NASA's figure for that stretch is about 170,000 years. Rising and sinking gas then carries it through the outer third of the Sun much faster. Neutrinos from the core, which hardly touch the gas, cross the whole Sun in about two seconds.

question: Through a telescope with a proper solar filter, sunspots look black against the Sun's glowing face. Yet a sunspot is still thousands of degrees hot. Why does it look dark?
answer: It is cooler, as its magnetism holds back heat from below
choices: It is cooler, as its magnetism holds back heat from below
It is cooler, as the fusion beneath it has died down
It is a gap in the glowing surface, showing a dark body below
It is the shadow of small moons crossing the Sun
context: Strong magnetic fields, thousands of times stronger than the quiet Sun's, choke off the rising and sinking gas that carries heat up to the surface, so a spot's dark centre is some 1,500 degrees or more cooler than the surface around it, about 5,500 degrees Celsius, and looks dim beside it; cut out and seen on its own, a sunspot would shine brighter than the full Moon. Fusion happens only in the core, far below. Christoph Scheiner took the spots for small moons, but Galileo showed in 1613 that they lie on the Sun's face and turn with it, and William Herschel later took them for holes in a glowing outer layer, showing a solid body beneath.

question: Heinrich Schwabe, a pharmacist in Dessau in Germany, watched the Sun on every clear day from 1826 to 1843. He hoped to catch an unknown planet, closer to the Sun than Mercury, crossing its face as a dark dot, and he noted down every sunspot he saw. He never found the planet. What did his record of the sunspots show?
answer: Their number rose and fell over about ten years
choices: Their number rose and fell over about ten years
Their number grew steadily over the seventeen years
Their number rose and fell with Mercury's trips round the Sun
Their number rose and fell with Earth's seasons
context: Schwabe reported a probable ten-year period in 1843; few noticed at first, but Rudolf Wolf took up regular counts, and the Royal Astronomical Society gave Schwabe its Gold Medal in 1857. The cycle is now measured at about 11 years on average, from just under 10 to just over 12, and it is a cycle of the Sun's magnetism: about every 11 years the Sun's magnetic poles swap places. Solar flares come most often near the cycle's peak.

question: Richard Carrington was drawing sunspots in England just before noon on 1 September 1859 when two patches of brilliant white light flared up among them, then faded within five minutes. About 17 hours later auroras glowed as far south as Cuba, and telegraph lines across Europe and North America threw sparks. On one line operators unhooked their batteries and still sent messages for two hours. What drove the current?
answer: Earth's changing magnetic field drove it along the wires
choices: Earth's changing magnetic field drove it along the wires
Charged particles from the Sun fell straight onto the wires
Charge left by the batteries still filled the long wires
Lightning from thunderclouds along the line struck the wires
context: A cloud of magnetised gas thrown out by the Sun struck Earth and set its magnetic field swinging, and a changing magnetic field drives currents along long wires, enough to shock operators and set paper alight. Carrington suspected that the flare had caused the storm but would not claim it from one case, writing that 'one swallow does not make a summer'. Flares are now known to be sudden releases of magnetic energy stored around sunspots, and a storm in March 1989 blacked out the power grid of Quebec for up to nine hours.

question: Margaret Burbidge, Geoffrey Burbidge, William Fowler and Fred Hoyle set out in 1957 how stars forge the chemical elements, over their long lives and in the supernova blasts that scatter what they made into space, where new stars and planets form from it. Most of the matter in a human body was made in stars. Which of the body's atoms were not?
answer: The hydrogen in its water
choices: The hydrogen in its water
The oxygen in its water
The carbon in its muscles
The iron in its blood
context: Hydrogen was made in the Big Bang, with helium and a little lithium, before any star shone, and it is the fuel that stars fuse into everything heavier, so the hydrogen in every water molecule in a body is older than the stars. The oxygen bonded to it in that water, like the body's carbon, was made by fusion inside stars, and much of its iron in supernovae long ago. Hydrogen is only about a tenth of a body's mass, though it makes up about six of every ten of its atoms.

question: At the very centre of the Sun, at about 15 million degrees Celsius, fusion runs slowly. Models put the heat it makes there at about 280 watts in each cubic metre, about as much as an active compost heap gives off and less than a person's body does, size for size. Why does the Sun shine so brightly all the same?
answer: Its core holds a vast amount of gas, all of it fusing
choices: Its core holds a vast amount of gas, all of it fusing
Its vast outer layers make far more heat than its core
Its gravity squeezes out far more heat than fusion
It still glows with heat stored up since its birth
context: Fusion happens only in the core, which reaches about a fifth to a quarter of the way from the centre to the surface, and that ball of gas is so vast that its slow output, cubic metre by cubic metre, adds up to all the Sun's light. Without fusion, the Sun's stored heat and slow shrinking together could have kept it shining only some tens of millions of years, as Lord Kelvin found.

question: Astronomers measure a galaxy's red shift from the dark lines in its spectrum, each of which marks one exact colour of light. In the light of one distant galaxy, every line has moved toward red, and every wave reaches Earth twice as long as when it set out. What do astronomers read from that doubling?
answer: Distances between galaxies have doubled since then
choices: Distances between galaxies have doubled since then
The galaxy itself has swelled to twice its size since then
The light has slowed to half its speed on the trip
Dust along the way has reddened the galaxy's light
context: Light's waves stretch with space itself as the universe expands, so waves twice as long mean that the distances between galaxies have doubled while the light was travelling: the universe was then half its present size. A galaxy itself does not swell, because its own gravity holds it together, and light's speed in empty space never changes. Dust reddens a galaxy's colour by soaking up more blue light than red, but it cannot move the lines; only a true red shift moves them.

question: Ralph Alpher and Robert Herman worked out in 1948 that the hot, dense young universe of George Gamow's theory should have left its heat behind as a faint glow, reaching Earth from every direction. That glow set out from gas thousands of degrees hot, yet they put it now at only about 5 degrees above absolute zero. Why should it be so cold by now?
answer: The universe's expansion has stretched its light
choices: The universe's expansion has stretched its light
Stars have soaked up most of its heat since then
The gas that sent it out has cooled down since then
Its heat has leaked out past the universe's edge
context: The expansion has stretched the glow's waves to about 1,100 times their length since it set out, some 380,000 years after the beginning, so light from gas at about 3,000 degrees above absolute zero now arrives as faint microwaves, at about 2.7 degrees. Once it set out, the glow crossed space freely, so neither the stars nor the gas's later cooling set its warmth, and there is no sign that the universe has an edge. Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson found the glow in 1964, near enough to the forecast, which had drawn almost no notice.

question: Fred Hoyle and his allies, who never accepted the Big Bang, held that the background glow was starlight soaked up and given off again by specks of dust in space. John Mather's team on the Cosmic Background Explorer (COBE) satellite, launched in 1989, measured the glow's brightness at each wavelength. It fitted almost perfectly the curve of a blackbody, the smooth glow that a perfect absorber of light gives off by its heat alone. Why did that fit count against the dust?
answer: Dust at many temperatures would blend many curves
choices: Dust at many temperatures would blend many curves
Dust gives off no light at the glow's wavelengths
Dust would glow in bright lines, not a smooth curve
Starlight passes through dust without warming it
context: A blackbody's curve is set by its temperature alone, whatever it is made of, and the glow matched one curve at 2.725 degrees above absolute zero to within 50 parts in a million; specks of dust scattered near and far, some warmer and some cooler, would add up to a blend that no single curve fits. Dust does soak up starlight, warming to between 10 and 100 degrees above absolute zero, and gives off a smooth glow at these wavelengths, so it fails for none of the other reasons. The Big Bang explains the pure curve as light that was once in balance with the hot, dense gas of the young universe.

question: Calculations of the universe's first few minutes predict that its ordinary matter came out about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass. Astronomers test the prediction in glowing clouds of gas in small galaxies that hold very few elements heavier than helium. Why do they choose such clouds?
answer: Stars have added the least helium to them
choices: Stars have added the least helium to them
Their weak gravity cannot pull in helium from outside
Heavy elements would hide the light of helium
Their helium has had the least time to leak away
context: Stars burn hydrogen into helium and also forge the heavier elements, so gas worked over by many stars carries extra helium, while clouds with almost no heavy elements are nearly as the first minutes left them. There the helium comes out near 24.5 percent by mass, close to the prediction, and the first minutes made about ten times more helium than all the stars since. Fred Hoyle himself, with Roger Tayler in 1964, argued that the universe holds too much helium for its stars to have made.

question: Every star, planet and cloud of gas that astronomers have ever seen is made of ordinary matter, the stuff of atoms. The Wilkinson Microwave Anisotropy Probe (WMAP), launched in 2001, and the European Planck satellite after it mapped the ripples in the background glow far more finely than before. How strong the ripples are at each size depends on what the universe is made of. How much of it does ordinary matter make up?
answer: About a twentieth
choices: About a twentieth
About a quarter
About half
Nearly all of it
context: Planck's map of 2013 put ordinary matter, the atoms, at about 4.9 percent, dark matter at about 26.8 percent and dark energy at about 68.3 percent, and the universe's age at 13.8 billion years; WMAP had found much the same. Dark matter's pull and dark energy's push show in what they do, but neither has been identified, so about 95 percent of the universe is stuff whose nature no one yet knows. The data hold an honest puzzle too: the expansion rate worked out from the glow disagrees with the rate measured from nearby galaxies.

question: Fritz Zwicky worked out in 1933, from the shifts in their light that Edwin Hubble and Milton Humason had measured, how fast the galaxies of the Coma Cluster, a swarm of more than a thousand, move about inside it. They darted about at some 1,000 kilometres a second, far faster than the gravity of all the cluster's stars could hold together. What did Zwicky conclude?
answer: Far more matter is there than can be seen
choices: Far more matter is there than can be seen
The cluster is flying apart and will scatter
Gravity pulls harder over such vast distances
The measured speeds must be far too high
context: Zwicky called the unseen stuff dunkle Materie, dark matter, and his idea was overlooked for decades. Modern studies confirm his inference and put dark matter at about nine-tenths of the cluster's mass, though what it is remains unknown. A few physicists still test a rival idea, that gravity itself works differently where its pull is very weak.

question: Vera Rubin and Kent Ford measured how fast glowing clouds of gas circle the centre of the Andromeda Galaxy, out to its edges, and reported in 1970. Around the Sun, which holds almost all of the Solar System's mass, Neptune circles far more slowly than Mercury. In Andromeda the outer clouds circle about as fast as the inner ones. What did that show about the galaxy's mass?
answer: Much of it lies far out, where little light shines
choices: Much of it lies far out, where little light shines
Nearly all of it sits in the bright centre
It is spread out through the disk just as its starlight is
There is less of it than its starlight suggests
context: If most of the mass sat in the bright centre, or were spread out as the starlight is, the outer clouds would circle more slowly, as Neptune does; keeping their speed means the mass inside their orbits keeps growing outward, so the galaxy must sit in a vast halo of unseen matter, five to ten times the mass that can be seen. Rubin and others found the same flat curves in galaxy after galaxy, 21 spirals in one study of 1980. Rubin herself did not rule out other explanations, and what dark matter is remains unknown: no detector has yet confirmed a particle of it.

question: A Type Ia supernova, the blast of one kind of exploding star, peaks at nearly the same brightness every time, so how bright one looks shows how far away it is. Saul Perlmutter's team, and a rival team with Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess, measured distant ones, expecting gravity to be slowing the universe's expansion. In 1998 both teams found the distant supernovae fainter than expected. What did they conclude?
answer: The expansion has been speeding up
choices: The expansion has been speeding up
The expansion has been slowing even faster
Dust between the galaxies had dimmed them
Such stars exploded more dimly long ago
context: Fainter meant farther: at the same red shift, the light had been travelling longer than a slowing expansion allows, so the universe grew more slowly long ago than it does now, and the expansion has been speeding up for the last 5 or 6 billion years. Astronomers correct for dust by the way it reddens light as it dims it, later studies found no strong sign that such stars were dimmer long ago, and maps of galaxies and of the background glow have since given the same answer. Perlmutter, Schmidt and Riess shared the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics, and the cause was named dark energy, but what it is, no one yet knows.

question: Johannes Kepler's best model of Mars fit almost every one of Tycho Brahe's sightings of the planet. Yet it missed some of them by eight arcminutes, about a quarter of the full Moon's width. Kepler threw the model out rather than let so small a gap pass. Why would he not accept the gap?
answer: Tycho's own errors were far smaller than the gap
choices: Tycho's own errors were far smaller than the gap
Ptolemy's old circles had missed by less than that
Tycho had checked every sighting through a telescope
Galileo's telescope had shown the same gap
context: Tycho, the last great astronomer to work without a telescope, fixed the planets' places to within about one or two arcminutes, so a miss of eight had to be the model's fault, not his; Kepler wrote that 'these eight minutes alone will lead us along a path to the reform of the whole of Astronomy.' Tables built on Ptolemy's circles had erred by more than 30 arcminutes, and Galileo first turned a telescope on the sky late in 1609, the year Kepler's Astronomia Nova came out.

question: Johannes Kepler spent years on Tycho Brahe's sightings of Mars, hunting for the true shape of the planet's path round the Sun. The shape he settled on, which he set out in his book Astronomia Nova in 1609, turned out to fit every planet. What did Kepler find?
answer: An ellipse, with the Sun off its centre
choices: An ellipse, with the Sun off its centre
An ellipse, with the Sun at its centre
A circle, with the Sun off its centre
An egg shape, with the Sun near its broad end
context: Kepler's first law: each planet moves on an ellipse with the Sun at one focus, one of two points that lie off the centre along the ellipse's long axis. Kepler tried an off-centre circle and an egg shape first, and each missed Tycho's sightings by about eight arcminutes, the two in opposite directions. The planets' ellipses are nearly round, so even Mars's path, drawn to scale, would look almost like a circle with the Sun a little off centre.

question: In the Northern Hemisphere, winter runs from the December solstice to the March equinox and lasts about 89 days. Summer, from the June solstice to the September equinox, lasts about 94. Earth passes nearest the Sun in early January. Why is the northern winter the shorter season?
answer: Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun
choices: Earth moves faster along its path when nearer the Sun
Earth spins faster on its axis when nearer the Sun
Earth's tilt shortens the season tipped away from the Sun
The winter season takes in February, the calendar's shortest month
context: By Kepler's second law the line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times, so a planet moves fastest when nearest the Sun: Earth, about 147 million kilometres away in early January, crosses its winter stretch of orbit a few days quicker than its summer stretch, when it is about 152 million kilometres away. The tilt makes the seasons but not this difference, since in the south, where winter falls between June and September, winter is the longest season. Earth's spin hardly changes through the year, and the solstice and the equinox are set by Earth's place on its path, however the calendar cuts up its months.

question: Saturn lies about ten times as far from the Sun as Earth does. Yet one trip round the Sun takes Saturn about 29 of Earth's years, not 10. Why does Saturn take so long?
answer: It moves more slowly, as the pull out there is weaker
choices: It moves more slowly, as the pull out there is weaker
It moves more slowly, as its great mass holds it back
It moves as fast as Earth, but on a far longer oval
It moves as fast as Earth, but winds along in small loops
context: Kepler's third law says the farther out a planet lies, the longer its year, and the year grows faster than the distance because the planet also moves more slowly: Saturn travels about 9.7 kilometres a second, a third of Earth's 29.8, on a path nearly as round as Earth's and tilted only 2.5 degrees from it. Newton explained why: the Sun's pull weakens with distance, and so weak a pull holds a planet on its curved path only at a slower speed. The small loops called epicycles belonged to the old models of Ptolemy and Copernicus, not to any planet's real path round the Sun.

question: Isaac Newton compared the Moon with a falling body, such as an apple. The Moon lies about 60 times as far from Earth's centre as the apple does. In each second it curves toward Earth, away from a straight path, by only about 1/3,600 of the distance the apple drops in its first second. What does that show about Earth's pull?
answer: It weakens with the square of the distance
choices: It weakens with the square of the distance
It weakens in step with the distance
It weakens with the cube of the distance
It weakens with the square root of the distance
context: Sixty times sixty is 3,600, so a pull that weakens with the square of the distance is 1/3,600 as strong at the Moon as at the ground, just what the Moon's fall of about 1.4 millimetres a second shows beside the apple's 4.9 metres. So twice as far from any mass its pull is a quarter as strong, and the pull that drops an apple is the same one that holds the Moon on its path. A pull weakening in step with the distance would leave a sixtieth of its strength at the Moon, sixty times too much.

question: Uranus kept drifting off the path that Newton's law of gravity gave it, running ahead of its predicted place for years and then falling behind. Urbain Le Verrier, in Paris, worked out what was causing the drift. Johann Galle turned a telescope in Berlin to the spot Le Verrier gave him on 23 September 1846, and Le Verrier was proved right. What had Le Verrier worked out?
answer: An unseen planet farther out was pulling on it
choices: An unseen planet farther out was pulling on it
An unseen planet nearer the Sun was pulling on it
An unseen moon of its own was tugging at it
A passing comet had knocked it off course
context: From the drift alone Le Verrier worked out where an unseen planet beyond Uranus had to be, as John Couch Adams did separately in England, and that night Galle and his assistant Heinrich d'Arrest found Neptune less than a degree from Le Verrier's spot. Some astronomers had wondered whether Newton's law failed so far from the Sun; instead the law had led to a new planet, showing that it held even at the edge of the known solar system.

question: Henry Cavendish hung a rod nearly 2 metres long from a thin wire, with a small lead ball at each end, and set a lead ball of about 158 kilograms beside each small one. From how far the wire twisted he measured how hard each big ball pulled its small ball sideways. He set that beside the small ball's weight, which is Earth's pull on it. What did comparing the two pulls let him work out?
answer: How many big balls' worth of mass Earth holds
choices: How many big balls' worth of mass Earth holds
How many big balls would fill Earth's whole volume
How dense the rock of Earth's crust is
How much harder lead pulls than rock does
context: A body's pull grows with its mass alone, whatever it is made of, so once the distances were allowed for, the two pulls set Earth's mass beside the big ball's; Cavendish gave the result in 1798 as Earth's average density, about 5.5 times that of water (he printed 5.48), using Earth's known size. The rocks of the crust are only about 2.7 to 3 times as dense as water, so Earth's deep inside must be far denser, evidence for a heavy metal core, and no hollow Earth, such as Edmond Halley had suggested in 1692, could hold so much mass.

question: Andrija Mohorovičić gathered the seismograph records of an earthquake that shook the Kupa Valley, in Croatia, on 8 October 1909, from 41 stations. Out to about 240 kilometres from the quake, each station recorded a single P-wave, the fastest kind of earthquake wave. Farther out, many stations recorded two P-waves, and the first to arrive was one that no nearer station had picked up. What did Mohorovičić conclude?
answer: Below a certain depth, rock carries the waves faster
choices: Below a certain depth, rock carries the waves faster
The quake broke twice, at two depths, moments apart
Below a certain depth, the rock is melted, like magma
Strong waves outrun weak ones over long distances
context: Waves that dipped into the faster rock below ran along it and climbed back up, and beyond about 240 kilometres they overtook the waves that stayed in the shallower rock, though their route was longer; Mohorovičić showed that the two were one kind of wave arriving by different paths. Two shocks would have sent two waves to the nearer stations too. He put the boundary about 54 kilometres down, and it is now called the Mohorovičić discontinuity, or Moho: the base of the crust.

question: A great earthquake sends two main kinds of wave through Earth. P-waves squeeze and stretch the rock along their path, while S-waves shake it from side to side. Seismographs across much of the far side of Earth record P-waves from the quake but no S-waves that have come straight through, and from that shadow seismologists concluded that the outer core is liquid. Why can an S-wave not cross a liquid?
answer: A liquid does not spring back when pushed sideways
choices: A liquid does not spring back when pushed sideways
A liquid's great density smothers any sideways shaking
A liquid's heat breaks up any sideways shaking
A liquid's particles sit too far apart to pass the wave on
context: An S-wave travels only through material that pushes back when it is sheared, as solid rock does; a liquid simply flows aside, so the wave dies out at the core's edge. A liquid does spring back when it is squeezed, which is why P-waves cross the outer core, though they slow down and bend where they enter it. The solid mantle just above the core is hot and dense, yet it carries S-waves.

question: Inge Lehmann, a Danish seismologist, studied the records of a strong earthquake in New Zealand in 1929. Earth's core was then thought to be liquid all through. It slows P-waves and bends them away from a wide shadow zone on the far side of the planet, yet two stations in Russia, well inside that zone, had recorded unusually strong P-waves from the quake. What did Lehmann propose in 1936 to explain them?
answer: A smaller core inside the core, where waves travel faster
choices: A smaller core inside the core, where waves travel faster
A smaller core inside the core, where waves travel more slowly
A layer at the bottom of the mantle, where waves travel faster
A layer at the top of the core, where waves travel more slowly
context: P-waves that reach the inner core speed up, and the change of speed at its edge bends some of them out into the shadow zone, where the Russian stations caught them. Beno Gutenberg, Charles Richter and Harold Jeffreys took up Lehmann's idea within a few years. Others argued from 1940 that the inner core is solid iron, and studies of the whole Earth ringing after great earthquakes confirmed by 1971 that it is solid.

question: Harry Hess's idea of sea-floor spreading, published in 1962, says that new ocean floor forms along the mid-ocean ridges and moves slowly away on either side. The drilling ship Glomar Challenger tested it across the ridge in the South Atlantic in 1968 and 1969, at sites from near its crest to more than 1,600 kilometres away. At each site, scientists dated the fossils in the lowest mud, the layer resting on the sea floor's rock. Which result would have counted most against Hess?
answer: The lowest mud about the same age at every site
choices: The lowest mud about the same age at every site
The lowest mud older at sites farther from the crest
The mud thin near the crest and thicker farther out
The ages climbing at the same pace on both sides
context: The first mud settles on new rock soon after it forms, so if the floor moves out from the crest, the lowest mud must be older the farther out it lies. It was: about 11 million years old at a site some 200 kilometres out and about 76 million at one more than 1,600 kilometres out, the floor moving away at about 2 centimetres a year, in step with the ages read from the sea floor's magnetic stripes. Mud of one age everywhere would have meant a sea floor made all at once.

question: Zircon crystals take in uranium as they grow but shut lead out, so any lead inside one was made there by the decay of its uranium. Uranium-235 decays into lead-207 with a half-life of about 700 million years. A geologist counts three atoms of lead-207 in a zircon for every atom of uranium-235 still left in it. How old is the crystal?
answer: About 1.4 billion years
choices: About 1.4 billion years
About 2.1 billion years
About 2.8 billion years
About 700 million years
context: Three lead atoms for every uranium atom left means a quarter of the uranium remains: half was gone after one half-life and half of the rest after a second, so two half-lives, about 1.4 billion years, have passed. Three lead atoms do not mean three half-lives, which would leave only an eighth, with seven lead atoms for every uranium atom. Because zircon starts with no lead, its clock begins at zero when the crystal forms.

question: Lord Kelvin worked out Earth's age in 1862 as the time a hot young planet would need to cool to its present state, reckoning back from how fast rock grows warmer with depth. He put it at 20 to 400 million years, and later at only 20 to 40 million. Pierre Curie and Albert Laborde found in 1903 that radium gives off enough heat to melt its own weight of ice in under an hour. Which of Kelvin's assumptions did that discovery undercut?
answer: That Earth makes no new heat of its own inside
choices: That Earth makes no new heat of its own inside
That Earth began as a ball of melted rock
That Earth's heat seeps out only through solid rock
That Earth's rock is alike all the way down
context: Rocks hold radioactive uranium, thorium and potassium, which make about half the heat now flowing out of Earth, so the planet cools far more slowly than Kelvin's sum allowed. His other flaw, pointed out by John Perry in 1895, was the rigid interior: rock deep inside slowly flows, carrying heat upward far faster than still rock can conduct it, and modern assessments count that the larger error. Radioactivity also gave a better clock, and Bertram Boltwood's uranium-lead ages of 1907 ran, once refined, from 410 million to 2.2 billion years.

question: Clair Patterson plotted the lead in five meteorites, three stony and two of iron, on a graph of one kind of lead against another. The five lay along one straight line, and its slope gave their age: about 4.55 billion years, he reported in 1956. He also measured the lead in mud from the deep-sea floor, and it fell on the very same line. What did that show?
answer: Earth formed at the same time as the meteorites
choices: Earth formed at the same time as the meteorites
The mud is as old as the meteorites are
Earth's own rocks are as old as the meteorites
Earth and the meteorites hold the same amount of lead
context: Deep-sea mud was taken to stand for the lead of Earth as a whole, and lying on the meteorites' line meant that Earth's lead had been building up from the same start for the same length of time. The line sets one kind of lead against another, not how much lead each sample holds, and it dates none of Earth's rocks: the mud itself is young, and Earth's oldest rocks, remade over the ages by moving plates and weathering, are only about 4 billion years old. Later work has moved Patterson's figure little: Earth's age is now given as 4.54 billion years, give or take 50 million.

question: Lead from the air and dust of his laboratory kept spoiling Clair Patterson's lead measurements until he built a clean room to keep it out. Robert Kehoe, chief medical adviser of the company that made the lead additive for petrol, held that lead in the human body is normal and that low levels do no harm. Patterson came to think that most of the lead in the air, and in people, was not natural at all. Which of his findings counted most against Kehoe?
answer: Recent snow in Greenland held far more lead than ancient snow
choices: Recent snow in Greenland held far more lead than ancient snow
Fresh snow in Greenland held lead that had fallen out of the air
Lead turned up even in the hair growing on his own head
Meteorites and the most ancient rocks held lead of their own
context: Snow piles up in yearly layers, so Greenland's ice keeps a dated record of the lead in the air, and the recent snow held some 200 times as much lead as snow that fell in ancient times. Lead in fresh snow, in hair or in old rocks shows only that lead is there, not when it came, so none of those finds could tell lead that had always been there from lead added since.

question: A planet's average temperature holds steady only while it sends as much energy out to space as it absorbs from sunlight. Norman Loeb, a NASA scientist, and his colleagues compared satellite measurements of both flows and reported in 2021 that Earth now absorbs more than it sends out, a gap that roughly doubled from 2005 to 2019. Where has most of the extra energy gone?
answer: Into the oceans
choices: Into the oceans
Into the air
Into the land
Into melting ice
context: By the reckoning of Karina von Schuckmann and her colleagues in 2023, about 89 percent of the heat Earth has gained since 1971 is in the oceans, about 6 percent in the land and about 4 percent has gone into melting ice, while only about 1 percent has warmed the air. Loeb's team checked the satellites against floats that measure how fast the oceans warm. While the imbalance lasts, Earth keeps gaining heat.

question: Milutin Milankovic, a Serbian engineer, spent nearly three decades working out, long before computers, how three slow cycles change the sunlight reaching Earth: the tilt of its axis, the stretch of its orbit and the wobble of its axis. He traced the sunlight at 65 degrees north, where the great ice sheets of the ice ages grew. By his reasoning, what lets such an ice sheet grow?
answer: Summers too cool to melt the winter's snow
choices: Summers too cool to melt the winter's snow
Winters cold enough to pile up heavier snow
Winters that come when Earth is farthest from the Sun
Years in which the total sunlight falls sharply
context: Snow that outlasts a cool summer piles up year after year into an ice sheet; Milankovic took the cool-summer idea from the climate scientist Wladimir Köppen. Heavier winter snow does little if the summer melts it all away, a hemisphere whose winter falls when Earth is farthest from the Sun has its summer at the nearest point and so a warmer one, and the cycles hardly change the sunlight the whole Earth gets in a year (the stretch of the orbit by about 0.2 percent) but shift it between seasons and places. His theory was largely ignored for about fifty years, and he died in 1958, before the deep-sea test of it.

question: Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted in June 1991, and its haze spread around the world high in the air. James Hansen's team at NASA ran the haze through a climate model and published a forecast early in 1992: the world would cool by about half a degree Celsius for a year or two, then warm again later in the decade. What did the world's thermometers show?
answer: A cooling of about the size the model forecast
choices: A cooling of about the size the model forecast
A cooling about twice the size the model forecast
A cooling that lasted decades, far past the forecast
No cooling at all, though the model forecast one
context: Global temperatures fell by about half a degree Celsius, and the journal Science reported early in 1993 that the forecast had been on target, though a later account notes that the model cooled the world a little too much. The cooling lasted one to three years. A forecast published before the event is a fair test of a model, because the answer cannot have been fitted to it afterwards.

question: Arctic sea ice shrinks every summer and grows back every winter. In a warm summer it shrinks further than usual and leaves wide stretches of open sea, and climate scientists say such a loss tends to speed itself up before the summer ends. What makes it do so?
answer: The dark water absorbs sunlight the ice would reflect
choices: The dark water absorbs sunlight the ice would reflect
The meltwater leaves the sea saltier, so it freezes less easily
The melting ice gives off heat that warms the sea around it
The sea water needs less heat than ice to warm up
context: Snow-covered ice reflects about 80 to 90 percent of the sunlight that strikes it and open sea less than a tenth, so each patch of ice lost lets in more heat and melts more ice. Melting in fact soaks up heat, sea ice is far less salty than sea water, and water needs about twice as much heat as ice to warm. A feedback like this one, or the extra water vapour that warmer air holds, strengthens a change that something else began, and other effects push back: after the record low of 2012, the 2013 summer ice was far larger.

question: Rock about 50 million years old on Ellesmere Island, in the Canadian Arctic, holds fossil alligators, giant tortoises and the wood and leaves of dawn redwood trees, where only tundra plants grow today. Oxygen in the animals' bones and teeth suggests that winters there rarely, if ever, froze. What best explains so warm an Arctic in that age, the Eocene?
answer: Earth as a whole was far warmer than it is now
choices: Earth as a whole was far warmer than it is now
The island lay near the equator and drifted north
Earth's axis stood nearly upright, with no seasons
The Sun shone far more brightly than it does now
context: The early Eocene was roughly 12 degrees Celsius warmer than before industry, with little or no ice anywhere and carbon dioxide estimated at about 700 to 1,600 parts per million, against about 430 today. Rock magnetism puts the island at about 75 to 80 degrees north then, close to where it lies now; the Moon keeps Earth's tilt between about 22 and 24.5 degrees; and the Sun, which brightens by about 1 percent every 110 million years, was a little dimmer. Antarctica's great ice sheet began to grow only about 34 million years ago, as the world cooled.

question: The Thames froze across at London in 24 winters between 1400 and 1831, and in the hardest frosts Londoners held fairs on the ice, the last in 1814. Those centuries fell in the Little Ice Age, a cool era that ended around 1850. Raphael Neukom's team compared records of past climate kept in tree rings, corals, ice cores and lake mud from around the world, and reported the result in 2019. What did the team find about when the cold came?
answer: Different regions were coldest in different centuries
choices: Different regions were coldest in different centuries
Every region was coldest in the same few decades
Only Europe cooled, while the rest of the world did not
